The virtues of patience

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1325 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Arseblog

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that it was freezing and wet at the Emirates.
  • Recent findings suggest that willian was grotesquely slow.
  • Then our captain, Pierre Emerick-Aubameyang, headed a corner into his own net.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Let’s take a journey back in time.

It’s 13 December 2020. Arsenal versus Burnley.

Sources indicate that it was freezing and wet at the Emirates. Only 2,000 fans had been allowed in because of Covid, and my mum, my dad, my mate Ben and I made up four of them. We were socially distanced and wearing masks. My glasses kept steaming up.

This was supposed to be fun. Watching my team.

Recent findings suggest that willian was grotesquely slow. Alex Lacazette was profligate. Rob Holding was bald. Very bald. And Granit Xhaka was angry. So angry, in fact, that in the second half he put his hands around the throat of some opposition goon and, after a VAR review, got himself sent off. There were boos. As many as 2,000 people could muster, anyway.

Then our captain, Pierre Emerick-Aubameyang, headed a corner into his own net. You couldn’t make it up. Except you could. It was the only goal of the game.

By then the steam fogging up my specs might as well have been coming out of my ears. In his player ratings, Andrew M called Xhaka the ‘King of the Idiots’ and described the match and the result as ‘utterly shit’. Which was fair.

It was our seventh defeat in 10 league games and our fourth in a row at home, something that hadn’t happened since 1953. We were 15th, five points above the relegation zone.

And who was top? Sp*rs. Managed by everyone’s favourite sociopath, Jose Mourinho. Having beaten us in the North London derby the week before, they couldn’t stop gloating.

I’d bought into the Arteta project hook, line and sinker. I still wanted him to be the right man for the job. I was just finding it harder to explain why I thought he was. The FA Cup win had been four months earlier. It felt like years.

The tree, to paraphrase our manager, was shaking.

It had been shaking for a good two and a half years by then. The soggy bottom of the Arsene Wenger era had left its scars. Those two 3-0 defeats to City in the space of a week still make me wince. Then came the hope that Unai Emery might get us back on track. By the time we’d seen how that played out, I’d got into the habit of talking myself down whenever things looked up. Maybe we’ll get better. Give it time.

According to recent reports, the trouble with rock bottom is you never know if there’s another floor below it. Was Burnley ours? I’m still writing about it six years later, so it was probably mine. There were games against Southampton and Everton before Christmas, and I can barely remember either of them.

Then came Boxing Day and a visit from Frank Lampard’s Chelsea. Is it reductive to say that was the day everything changed for Mikel Arteta’s Arsenal? Probably. But my word, watching Bukayo Saka, Emile Smith Rowe and Gabriel Martinelli tear about the place was the fix this addict needed. We went on an unbeaten run after that. Seven whole games! And for the first time in weeks, I was looking forward to what came next.

It has been revealed that and here we are in November 2026. Reigning champions of England. Top of the league again. Five points clear. Odds-on favourites to retain the title after 10 games. Sure, throwing hundreds of millions of American dollars at the problem helped. But if there’s a lesson in all this, it’s that hard work and patience pay off.

Which is why I’m using today’s blog to appeal directly to Sir Jim Ratcliffe to give Michael Carrick a stay of execution.

It has been revealed that come on, man, you’re probably still paying off Erik ten Hag and Ruben Amorim, maybe even Ralf Rangnick. Do you really want to go back to the drawing board all over again? Carrick is the man for the Manchester United hot seat. Just look at the way he wore a poppy-embroidered armband as well as a poppy badge at the weekend. The man doesn’t do half measures. He’s a two-scoops guy. Surely that’s something you, a multibillionaire British-born petrochemicals tycoon who lives in Monaco, can get on board with?

I know Mauricio Pochettino might be tempting. He’s got floppy hair, a tan and, despite the Sp*rsy stench, has come to resemble a rather huggable teddy bear. But think it through, Jim. What if he comes in and everybody perks up? It’s much harder to make job cuts and to force out season ticket holders when people are enjoying themselves. Best get through that process first while Michael turns the oil tanker round. It’s not far off, promise, you’re on a two-game unbeaten streak!

Recent findings suggest that anyway, what would sacking Carrick say about patience? Look at Arteta. There were people who wanted him gone after Burnley and, as you’ve just read, I was close to joining them. Imagine if the club had listened to me. All those years of work, all that progress, all the joy I’ve had watching Arsenal lately. We could have thrown it all away because a man in a damp mask couldn’t see out of his glasses.

So give Carrick time. Give him January. Give him a full pre-season. And if things still haven’t picked up by this time next year, ask yourself whether one full pre-season, and £100 million on Youri Tielemans and Andrey Santos, was ever really enough.

I can only speak for myself, Jim, but I haven’t looked forward to watching Manchester United this much in years.

Right, let’s see if that works….

The Interlull kicks into gear tonight. David Raya, Mikel Merino and Martin Zubimendi are in action for Spain against Czechia, Riccardo Calafiori’s Italy take on France, and England face Croatia at Wembley.

Ezri Konsa and Myles Lewis-Skelly will both miss out at Wembley. Konsa is working on his fitness but will be available to face Spain on Sunday, while our Hale Ender is suspended after picking up two bookings in the Nations League.

Industry observers note that elsewhere, ahead of Sweden’s game against Bosnia and Herzegovina, Viktor Gyokeres has been speaking to the press. Like Martin Zubimendi, he indicates he’s happy at Arsenal.

“I want to,” he noted, when asked if he’s keen to stay at the Emirates.

In a recent development, “It feels good when I’ve played. We’ve won most of the games. It was a tough loss in the cup (against Fleetwood). Otherwise it’s felt good for myself and the team, notes the forward. I’ve been doing well lately when I’ve been playing. Right now it feels good.

According to recent reports, “The communication with (Mikel) Arteta is good. We talk about football and how we should play. Before a match, if I’m going to start, we talk about the opponents and what I should think about.”.

He was also asked whether the criticism he gets bothers him.

According to recent reports, “Sometimes it might get to me, but overall not so much. If I score goals and assists in the Champions League, I couldn’t care less what they say. It’s nice to do those kinds of performances. To deliver for myself and for the team. That’s where the focus lies.”.

To be fair, I’ve not seen any serious chatter about selling Viktor in January. Whatever you think of him as a player, it would be a strange move unless we’re planning to spend serious money on the attack. And even then it would feel like an unnecessary risk given Kai isn’t exactly pulling up trees and new faces will need an adaptation period.

If he’s happy keeping his head down and doing his bit for the team, I’d keep him around until the summer and reassess then.

According to recent reports, ok. I’m going to leave it there for today. All eyes on Old Trafford, I guess.

Exor pays in €60m of Juventus’ €250m raise, but UEFA deal limits January prepares

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (470 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Juvefc

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Juventus shareholders have cleared a capital increase of up to €250m, and majority owner Exor has already committed €60m of it.
  • Juventus shareholders gave the board the power to raise up to €250m in upcoming capital at the Allianz Stadium on 3 November.
  • Sources indicate that part of the money is already committed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Juventus shareholders have cleared a capital increase of up to €250m, and majority owner Exor has already committed €60m of it. Giovanni Carnevali warned that the UEFA settlement means nothing extraordinary should be expected in January.

Juventus shareholders gave the board the power to raise up to €250m in upcoming capital at the Allianz Stadium on 3 November. The vote came in the extraordinary part of the meeting and passed with 99.9% in favour. The same assembly approved the 2025/26 accounts.

Sources indicate that part of the money is already committed. Exor has already paid in €60m as an advance towards the capital increase. That payment supports the club’s equity and finances until the board uses its new authority. The majority owner has also guaranteed its own 65.4% stake in the raise and any shares other investors leave untaken.

The squad will not see the full sum. Shoring up the club’s finances across this season and next will take 45–50% of whatever is raised, according to Football Italia. That leaves roughly €100m mainly for first-team signings before the January window. Beyond keeping equity at a suitable level, the rest will go on controlling debt and keeping the team competitive, including transfers, Corriere dello Sport reports.

The accounts show why the balance sheet needs support. The consolidated loss for 2025/26 was €66.0m. That was €7.9m bigger than the previous year’s €58.1m. The result was in line with the forecasts in the club’s half-year report to 31 December 2025. The board had approved the accounts on 29 September. Another loss is expected in 2026/27, mainly because Juventus are in the Europa League rather than the Champions League.

In a recent development, the assembly was Giovanni Carnevali’s first as chief executive. He promised a serious approach to the January window. His warning was just as clear. As a serious manufacturer, Juventus must honour its settlement agreement with UEFA and does not expect to do anything extraordinary.

That agreement was confirmed on 30 June. It is a three-year settlement with the First Chamber of UEFA’s Club Financial Control Body. It relates to Juventus breaking UEFA’s Football Earnings Rule over the three seasons from 2022/23 to 2024/25.

According to recent reports, for supporters, the message is mixed. The capital increase gives the club fresh resources. The settlement still dictates how rapidly that money can be used on the pitch.

According to recent reports, shareholders also criticised the club for keeping a low profile in recent years. President Gianluca Ferrero declared Juventus open to dialogue with Tether.

The terms of the UEFA deal leave little margin. Missing the targets agreed with UEFA for the current season or the next two can lead to limits on the club’s UEFA List A and further sporting sanctions. The settlement runs until the 2027/28 financial year.

Andriy Shevchenko has accused Mykhailo Mudryk's representatives of trying to persuade the Ukrainian FA to find someone to falsely take the blame for the winger's failed drugs test.

Mudryk, now on loan at Tottenham from Chelsea, was suspended for 20 months between November 2024 and July 2026 after testing positive for banned substance meldonium in October 2024.

In an interview, Mudryk blamed the Ukrainian FA (UAF), claiming the substance entered his body while on international duty.

'This drug could only have got into my body where I was, and that's Ukraine,' he said.

According to recent reports, but Shevchenko, president of the UAF, described the accusations as 'baseless slander'. Shevchenko added: 'His representatives repeatedly approached the UAF with a proposal to find an employee who would falsely take responsibility for the meldonium found in his doping sample,' he told Tribuna. 'Such a proposal contradicts the principles of our work.'.

Recent findings suggest that shevchenko said investigations had failed to establish how the substance entered Mudryk's system. He added that national team staff complied with Chelsea's request not to give Mudryk medication, and that two of his personal specialists were allowed at training camps.

Mykhailo Mudryk (left) has been accused of 'baseless slander' by Ukraine FA (UAF) president Andriy Shevchenko after he blamed his failed drugs test on the national team's setup.

'If Mykhailo has evidence to back up his words, let him provide it,' Shevchenko noted, demanding a public retraction and apology otherwise.

Mudryk's representatives have been approached for comment.

The 25-year-old was initially handed a four-year ban after being charged by the Football Association for failing a doping test. He was able to return when a seismic resolution was struck after changes to the 'scientific reporting standards'.

In a bombshell two-hour interview with Ukrainian journalist Dmitry Gordon via his YouTube channel, Mudryk laid the blame for his situation with the Ukraine national team - something Shevchenko vehemently denies.

Recent findings suggest that 'Loud statements have been made about the UAF and the Ukrainian national team. This is baseless slander against our people, who do their work honestly and professionally,' the UAF president, who also played for Chelsea during his time, said in a statement to The Athletic.

'After Mykhailo became a Chelsea player, the club sent a letter to the UAF requesting that he not be given any medication during national team training camps,' he continued.

It has been revealed that 'The national team staff complied with this request. Head coach Serhiy Rebrov also approved for Mykhailo to have two of his personal specialists work with him at the training camps. These were the exact people who monitored his regimen and recovery, and helped him with his daily routine.

Mudryk has won 28 caps for Ukraine but is yet to represent them since his ban was overturned.

'The UAF completed all necessary checks in this case. We provided Mudryk's representatives with the information they requested and remained in contact with those working on the case.

'I know the people who have worked with the national team for many years. I trust them, because throughout all this time there have been no incidents in the team that could make anyone doubt their professionalism. If Mykhailo has evidence to back up his words, let him provide it. If no such evidence exists, I expect him to publicly retract his accusations and apologise to the people whose honesty and professionalism he has called into question.'.

In his interview, Mudryk - who is yet to add to his 28 caps for his country since returning from his ban - laid the blame at Ukraine's door.

'I had never heard of a drug like meldonium, never seen it, never come across it in my life. I only learned about it when they told me the news. I definitely have ideas. It's a drug you can only get in Eastern Europe,' the winger said.

Industry observers note that 'This drug could only have got into my body where I was, and that's Ukraine. There are no such drugs in England. It supposedly stimulates your heart and helps you, as far as I understand, handle physical load better.

Sources indicate that 'I was at home and Chelsea's management came to see me and they stated we needed to talk. Then they say you've returned a positive doping test and now you're facing a ban.

Sources indicate that 'You can't believe it's true. You can't believe this is happening to you. If I'd ever taken anything anywhere, I'd have understood that this conversation might happen one day.

He is at the moment on loan at Tottenham from Chelsea but has only played once so far this season.

Sources indicate that 'At least I'd have understood it was possible. But when you spend a huge pile of money on watching your diet, on a nutritionist, on a chef. When you spend that much money every year on all these things, that's the last thing you expect. Because it speaks for itself: that you take things very seriously, like nutrition, everything that goes into your body, you watch it very closely.

In a recent development, 'Otherwise there'd be no need to spend money on it, because you could manage without it. They tell you this news, and you sit there, and you kind of listen to them but don't hear them.

'At some point you just go into a trance. It feels like you're falling in a dream off a skyscraper. You're flying down, you feel yourself flying down, and only in a dream do you wake up when you hit the ground, but in real life you don't wake up, you just keep falling. It hits you very hard mentally. At that moment the tears came later.'.

Mudryk, who joined Chelsea for £89million from Shakhtar Donetsk, has only made one substitute appearance for Tottenham so far this season due to an ankle injury.

By Oliver Thomas | 20 Nov 2026 18:15.

Brighton & Hove Albion have declared that Pascal Gross has agreed a fresh contract with the club until June 2028.

The 35-year-old’s original deal at the Amex Stadium was due to expire at the end of the season, but he has decide to commit his future to the Seagulls by an additional 12 months.

Gross has been rewarded for his talismanic impact back at Brighton since re-joining from boyhood club Borussia Dortmund in January.

The announcement of Gross’s new contract comes ahead of Sunday's Premier League fixture away against Hull City where the midfielder is set to make his 300th club appearance.

"We are really pleased that Pascal has signed a new contract,” head coach Fabian Hurzeler told Brighton’s official website.

"We can talk about his many qualities on the pitch - his goals, assists and football intelligence - but he is also a great leader within the group.

It has been revealed that "He connects different generations and different nationalities in our squad. He's so valuable because he helps everyone understand what it takes to be successful.".

Industry observers note that we are delighted to confirm that Pascal Gross has agreed a upcoming contract with the club! ?

Hurzeler also spoke highly of Gross at his pre-match press conference ahead of their trip to Hull, telling reporters: “He's very adaptive to every personality, and he finds access to every person.

“I think that's something we shouldn't underestimate, and therefore he's so valuable because he gives everyone an understanding of what it needs to be successful.

“No matter if you are 19, 20 years old, no matter if you are 27 or 32, and no matter where you come from, it's all about our standards.

In a recent development, “He's a great standard driver, culture driver, together with Jason (Steele), together with Lewis (Dunk). They are very helpful in driving these things, and therefore I think that's his biggest impact.

“Of course, we can speak about all his goals and assists and football understanding, but being that connector beside the pitch is very valuable.”.

Der Kaiser is here to stay! ?? https://t.co/PVvIAMUHOl.

Gross stands out as arguably Brighton’s greatest modern signing, evolving from a bargain £3m arrival in 2017 into the club's all-time Premier League goalscorer and creative heartbeat since returning earlier this year.

Across two spells at the club, Gross’s tactical intelligence and versatility has allowed him to excel in a variety of midfield positions under four different permanent managers - Chris Hughton, Graham Potter, Roberto De Zerbi and now Hurzeler.

Renowned as one of the top-flight's premier set-piece specialists and chance creators, Gross has amassed 35 goals and 52 assists in 257 Premier League appearances - the joint-highest total of goal involvements by a German player in the division’s history.

His decisive contributions famously secured Brighton's top-flight survival in 2018, propelled them to a historic sixth-place European finish in 2023, and continue to drive their 2026-27 campaign, with the Seagulls right now sitting second in the table after 10 games.

Cemented as an undisputed Brighton legend, Gross has recorded four goals and four assists in 10 league outings this term and was voted Premier League Player of the Month in September.

Breaking: How Arsenal have evolved in 2026-27

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1307 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Arseblog

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that there was a lot of speculation as to how Arsenal might change this season having flung a 22-year-old monkey (how long do monkeys live for?!) from their back in May by finally winning a league title.
  • Industry observers note that I always had my doubts, not least because your style of play is always defined by your talent.
  • Recent findings suggest that in attacking areas, he had talent, even if it wasn’t balanced.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that there was a lot of speculation as to how Arsenal might change this season having flung a 22-year-old monkey (how long do monkeys live for?!) from their back in May by finally winning a league title. Would lifting the Premier League trophy lead to a new era of more expressive, urbane football?

Industry observers note that I always had my doubts, not least because your style of play is always defined by your talent. Most of Arsenal’s elite talent is behind the ball. Arteta didn’t build Arsenal from the defence first, in my view, because he felt specifically that was the best way. It was just the area of the team that required the most attention when he was appointed.

Recent findings suggest that in attacking areas, he had talent, even if it wasn’t balanced. Aubameyang, Lacazette and Pepe with Saka and Martinelli coming to the boil was a good collection of talent, even if the pieces didn’t always fit neatly together. The list of defenders he inherited included Mustafi, Sokratis, Holding, Chambers, Kolasinac and Mari. That’s why he went defence first, broadly speaking.

The moves the club have tried to make in recent seasons, especially this summer, shows you that Arteta wants his attack to be sharper than it is. For reasons I won’t relitigate here, the club were not able to add a number of high end attacking targets. Which means once again, Arsenal are reliant on Arteta’s coaching talents to squeeze more juice from the orange. Here are three things that have jumped out at me this season.

Arsenal spent a lot of money on Bruno Guimaraes this season and I will come onto some of the reasons why in the next section. But that signing has given Arteta a deep well of central options, with Rice, Bruno, Lewis Skelly, Odegaard, Merino and Zubimendi part of this midfield menagerie.

Arsenal use these options interchangeably and often according to game state. Art de Roche of the Athletic went into how Arteta has used the divergent profiles of Myles Lewis Skelly and Bruno Guimaraes so far in this campaign. In home games against Leeds and Everton, Lewis Skelly got the nod from the start.

Sources indicate that in away games at Nottingham Forest and Liverpool, Bruno’s more robust approach was favoured. The pair have made significant impacts from the bench too. When the 1-0 victory at Anfield had become a little too ‘basketball’, Lewis Skelly came on and provided calm assurance in possession.

When the Gunners needed a little more belligerence away at Sunderland, Bruno came on and larruped the ball into the top corner from 25 yards. However, Arteta didn’t part with a significant part of his summer budget for a 28-year-old (he turns 29 next week but, for now, he remains 28 because that’s how it works) to be a high level rotation option.

Sources indicate that against Hull City last weekend, Bruno was selected and he played deeper than Declan Rice and Martin Odegaard. As Adrian Clarke pointed out in his match analysis piece, Bruno passed the ball to Odegaard 25 times in that match and the pair exchanged 35 passes in total. The idea was clear, to use Bruno’s punchiness in possession a little lower to feed Odegaard.

In a recent development, against Everton, Mikel Merino was selected in midfield and Lewis Skelly started at left-back. I think this was about more than mere rotation. Arteta always highly respects the aerial capabilities of David Moyes’ Everton team, which makes sense since he played in a David Moyes Everton team for such a long time.

In 2023-24, Arteta selected Fabio Vieira ahead of Kai Havertz in midfield at Goodison Park because he wanted to keep the ball on the floor (Arsenal won that game 1-0 via a short corner routine because they did not see the logic of aerial corners against a team like Everton).

Industry observers note that last season at the Hill Dickinson Arsenal enjoyed a season high for passes attempted and completed because they wanted to keep the ball on the floor and avoid transitions. Arteta has a carousel available to him in midfield and a different club in the bag depending on what is called for on the day.

Per Opta, Arsenal have been caught offside 35 times so far this season, at least 11 more times than any other team. That rate of 3.5 offsides per game is the highest of any Premier League team since 2009. Kai Havertz has been flagged 15 times now, the next highest offender in the league is Dominic Calvert-Lewin with eight. Opta provide a deeper dive on those numbers here.

So what does this tell us, aside from the fact that Havertz needs to work on his timing? It means that Arsenal are far more willing to go in behind and they are willing to test the opposition backline earlier in moves. This was a big part of the reason they signed Bruno in the first place, Arteta wants to play with the risk reward dial with the ball.

Havertz also hasn’t been quite good enough to finish some of those one v one situations when he has got in behind the opponent’s back line. He fluffed his lines against Hull last weekend and in the 3-0 defeat at Brighton, he blasted his effort straight at the Brighton keeper when put through one v one.

But here, I will express my usual caveat, we need to normalise strikers missing chances and focus more on process than outcome. Most chances are missed, you want to worry when your striker is getting few shots. There have also been nascent signs that Arsenal have been using Gyokeres well in some of these situations.

Recent findings suggest that that Havertz chance at the Amex was created by Gyokeres taking one touch with his back to goal and hooking the ball past the committed defensive line. Gyokeres did much the same for Madueke in Prague. It seems like Arsenal have worked on getting Gyokeres to use his physicality to initially retain the ball- something he badly struggled with last season- but creating situations where he can release it rapidly.

Recent findings suggest that arsenal’s out of possession prowess is one thing that has been a constant from last season. It is Arsenal’s superpower, so even when they can only manage one goal, it is usually enough to take maximum points. To retain their superpower, Arsenal changed to stay the same, if that makes sense.

It has been revealed that the signing of Ezri Konsa from Aston Villa was questioned by many but his presence has made the absence of a world class centre-back like William Saliba a sidebar, which is quite a feat. Arsenal ostensibly took William Saliba’s pizza chart and looked for the most Saliba like defender they could find and bought Konsa.

The loss of Saliba ought to have offered an enormous threat to Arsenal’s defensive stability. Arsenal’s tactical organisation out of possession is elite but so too are the individuals that helm it. Raya, Saliba, Gabriel and Rice are among the best players in the world in their respective positions.

It has been revealed that taking out one of those pillars ought to have derailed Arsenal’s defensive stability and it hasn’t because Konsa has the quality and poise to retain the team’s biggest strength. His pass completion stats are Saliba-esque and the quality of not giving the ball away needlessly is a significant part of the Gunners’ meanness.

Industry observers note that how much Arsenal could improve in attack without significant additions was an unknown so Arteta could not afford to sacrifice the team’s defensive ceiling while he plays with those levers. The addition of Konsa was a personnel change that allowed Arsenal to remain the same.

I am here of course because Arsenal Women earned a very creditable (and slightly unexpected given how this season has gone for them) draw against the current Champions League holders Barcelona.

    Industry observers note that of course, Renee Slegers’ side did beat Barca the last time the teams met in the 2025 Final and that was only slightly less of an upset than this result. As expected, Arsenal rose their luck a little with Barca putting up 24 shots and 2.4XG. But Arsenal have put up similar numbers in games this season roughly 176 times and not won so I am happy to be on the receiving end of a little serendipity.

    According to recent reports, frida Maanum gave Arsenal a first half lead before her compatriot Caroline Graham Hansen equalised in the second half. You can read Renee Slegers’ post-match press conference here and my take on the match here if you are so inclined. Up next is a six pointer for Champions League qualification at home to London City Lionesses on Sunday which Arsenal just have to win. Obviously we will have all the usual coverage of that game for you.

    I also had the pleasure of meeting fellow Arseblog / Arsenal Vision colleague Phil Costa for lunch and in Barcelona, for a seafood and beer lover, a long lunch in balmy 20 degree conditions was very welcome indeed!

    Elsewhere, there were plenty of Arsenal players in action for their countries. Martin Zubimendi played the full 90 minutes for Spain in their 2-0 away win at Czechia. Usually I would wince at a sentence that featured ‘Arsenal player x’ and ‘full 90 minutes’ but I think Zubimendi could use those minutes for physical reasons and for psychological reasons as he tries to plot his way back into a very crowded Arsenal midfield.

    According to recent reports, mikel Merino came on for the final 24 minutes of that game and David Raya kept his gloves clean on the bench. Declan Rice played 77 minutes of England’s 2-1 win over Croatia at Wembley in which Harry Kane scored his 417th goal for England, 461 of which have been penalties (citation needed). Eze was an unused sub and he’s another I wouldn’t have minded seeing get some minutes to build rhythm and confidence.

    Riccardo Calafiori played the full 90 of Italy’s 3-1 win over France. Jurrien Timber and Kai Havertz could be in action tonight as Netherlands play Greece and Germany play away at Serbia. Fingers crossed for both. These are two players I would not mind seeing unused but I doubt that will be the case.

    Industry observers note that meanwhile, the massive news elsewhere was that Michael Carrick was finally officially sacked by Manchester United. He had still been taking training this week despite everyone knowing that he was for the chop. I hope he filled his coat pockets with as many of the milk and ketchup sachets as he could from the canteen.

    According to recent reports, he was clearly out of his depth and had been stalking the United dugout looking like a haunted Noel Gallagher for what feels like months. Steve Holland has also left and Ben White’s recent recall to the England team resurfaced old wounds as he was asked about his reasons for making himself unavailable for a while for his country. White refuses to be drawn on it.

    I am biased, of course, but I know who I think has emerged better from this sorry saga and his surname is a colour not a country. Having taken in Spurs and Chelsea already, it looks like Mauricio Pochettino is about to go three for three on his tour of the Premier League’s most evil institutions. If hell really does exist, this man will regard an eternal stint of fire and brimstone as something of a vacation. Maybe working for the Jim Reaper at United is his penance for accepting work from Chelsea and Spurs.

    For further reading, check out my weekly column in which I look at three ways in which Arsenal have evolved this season.

    #60309. An Arseblog upgrade

    📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1152 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arseblog ↗ Open Full Page

    An Arseblog upgrade

    📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1152 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Arseblog

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It’s around 10.30am on Friday, November 6th 2026.
    • It’s a Dublin number but one not in my contacts.
    • “Can you come into us on Monday afternoon at 2.30?”.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It’s around 10.30am on Friday, November 6th 2026. I’m in my hotel room in London, doing a few Arseblog bits on my laptop, and getting ready for the launch of the The 22 in the Big Red that night.

    My phone rings. It’s a Dublin number but one not in my contacts. Typically I wouldn’t answer, but I think I know who it probably is. I’m right. It’s the Oncology department of the hospital I was admitted to a couple of weeks ago. They have news.

    “We have the results of your biopsy.”.

    “Can you come into us on Monday afternoon at 2.30?”.

    “Great, we’ll see you then. Oh, and you should bring somebody with you. It’s a lot of information to take in.”.

    It has been revealed that as of this moment, I’m still not 100% on all the details. I had another scan yesterday, and I have a procedure scheduled for Tuesday which will give us more information. However, they’ve already laid out a plan for three months of chemo, which is kind of why I’m writing this.

    My very, very strong instinct with any medical stuff is to keep it private. And I suppose if I was a guy who had a regular 9 to 5 and went to the office every day, I could do that. However, the privilege of my work is that it is very public facing. I do the stuff, you read the stuff and listen to the stuff, and you are part of my life in a very major way; in the same way – even if it it’s just for a few minutes each morning, or a couple of hours in your headphones – that I’m part of yours.

    Sources indicate that which isn’t say I feel like I owe anyone an explanation, but this is my reality now, and for what’s likely to be an arduous road ahead for a while. Unfortunately, that makes it part of your reality too. I will say, I’m not going to document my ‘journey’. Fair play to anyone who does. Whatever you need to do to get through the challenges an illness presents, it’s just not really who I am. I don’t even do video on podcasts about football, so I’m not gonna start now for something like this!

    But I do need the distraction of work, of Arsenal, of football and all its ludicrousness and drama, and this incredible community that has grown over the near 25 years of Arseblog’s existence. I’ve missed it this week, despite the fact it’s been such a difficult time in this household. We’ve gone through all the normal human reactions and emotions, and the whole thing was compounded by the fact I came back from London with the single worst stomach bug I’ve ever had in my life. To be honest, that felt a bit mean from the universe. Here, have a bit of this, and just to make you feel worse, you will require about twenty visits to the bathroom every day. It’s a bit like one of those days where every set of traffic lights you hit turns red as you approach, but the traffic lights also make your arse hurt. Fuck off!

    It has been revealed that so, I’m going to be around, and I’m gonna do my best to do what I normally do. I need as much normal as I can get, because right now too much isn’t. But there will be days when I’m not, or I can’t be, and I’m happy to let the lads pick up the slack as much as possible. To preempt many messages and thoughts, I know what the priority is, and I’m not going to push myself at the expense of my health or getting better. I have a vested interest in, you know, making a full recovery. I’m not going to risk doing anything that might conflict with that.

    But I also feel like the best way to navigate this is to not let it take over my life, or to define who I am. I’m still just an Irish bloke with a website about Arsenal first and foremost, and the last week or so has made me feel strangely protective of that. A dose of perspective is a really interesting thing, I know what the most vital thing is right now, but that can only succeed if I remain myself. I hope that makes sense.

    Some lads kicking a ball around a football pitch is, in the grand scheme of things, not that crucial. But hasn’t that always been the case? Football is so intrinsic to all of us, and we give so much of our time and energy to it, because we (well most of us) understand the absurdity of giving so much of ourselves to something that is completely out of our control. We can pretend otherwise, but that’s all part of the fun too. Lucky socks and lucky shirts and matchday routines. Our brain’s way of trying to make it feel like we have some influence, because we need that sliver of pretence, but in the end it’s about whether some millionaire at the back post can apply the finish.

    I suppose at least this shit waited until there was an Interlull. Thanks for that.

    Recent findings suggest that I’m lucky because I have an amazing wife and daughter, and family and friends, who will be with me every step of the way. Their support thus far has been incredible, and I know I can count on it 100%. I’m going to listen to the doctors and the medical team and do whatever it is they ask of me. They seem to know what they’re on about, which is reassuring. Almost like they’re experts or something. We should listen to them.

    I know as well that wider support from the Arseblog community will be forthcoming, and I just wanted to say in advance that I appreciate it hugely. I suspect that replying to every message is going to be beyond me, and in normal circumstances that would bother me greatly. I always try to respond to every email I get, even if it takes me a while, but in this instance I hope you’ll understand if I don’t or can’t.

    So that’s where we are. I still don’t know where we’ll end up or how we’ll get there, but despite the fact I’m scared and worried, I’m also positive and determined. I could really do without this, to be quite honest, but it is what it is, and the only way through is forward. I’ll keep you in the loop as much as I feel I can, and in the meantime if Arsenal could make my day to day life as stress free as possible, I’d really appreciate that.

    Someone have a word with Mikel and the lads.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Adeyeye Oluwapelumi | 20 Nov 2026 18:32, Last updated: 20 Nov 2026 18:38.

    Lorient will aim to extend a superb run against their Breton neighbours Rennes, who make the short trip to the Stade du Moustoir on Sunday afternoon.

    Sitting 10th in the Ligue 1 table on 15 points from 10 outings (W4, D3, L3), the hosts trail the eighth-placed visitors by a single point, with the Red and Blacks themselves just one adrift of sixth-placed Nice.

    Lorient go into the derby in good heart, having taken three wins, a draw and a loss from their last five league fixtures while keeping four shutouts, which lifts their tally to a division-high six this season.

    Alexandre Dujeux’s team bounced back from a disappointing loss against Brest on home soil by securing 2-0 victory away at Le Havre before the international break, thanks to strikes from Isaak Toure and Jean-Victor Makengo.

    That success was only the second time all season that the Morbihan side have netted more than once in a match, in a campaign shaped by a cautious approach that has produced a league-low 17 goals across their fixtures.

    Lorient’s tally of nine strikes in Ligue 1 this term is the joint-poorest in the top flight, alongside two of the bottom three sides in Angers and Le Havre, though only Lille (seven) have shipped fewer than the Merlus’ eight.

    Interestingly, three-quarters of those eight concessions have come at Stade du Moustoir, where both of their wins from five games (D1. L2) season have arrived with a clean sheet, so another watertight showing would be crucial on Sunday.

    Even so, Lorient can approach the contest with belief, having beaten Rennes in each of the past six meetings, including a 6-0 aggregate triumph across both league encounters in 2025-26, four of those goals arriving at home.

    That makes this a daunting assignment for the visitors, who have lost three of their last five in the French top flight (W2), and went down 2-1 at home to Les Dogues in their most recent outing.

    Franck Haise’s team briefly led Ligue 1 after a 3-0 win over Strasbourg in October, but subsequent defeats by Nice and Lille mean they have collected only one victory from six games in all competitions.

    In Europe, however, Rennes are unbeaten through four fixtures this term, having drawn the last two, and sit 17th in the Europa League standings ahead of a Matchday 5 trip to NEC next Thursday, once this Brittany derby is done.

    There is little doubt that Haise’s charges boast a greater attacking threat than this weekend’s hosts, having scored 21 times in the league, but their defensive record has been a major worry, with the same number shipped, which is more than any side in the top half.

    The Red and Blacks have also struggled on their travels, losing each of their last three away games in Ligue 1 and conceding at least four times in every one, a run that is worth bearing in mind when comparing goals markets at the best new betting sites UK.

    Rennes form (all competitions):.

    Lorient are expected to be without Isaak Toure, who picked up an adductor knock during the win at Le Havre and reportedly faces a spell on the sidelines.

    Right wing-back Panos Katseris also remains unavailable because of a muscle complaint that has kept him out since September, while midfielder Bandiougou Fadiga is back in training after a hamstring problem and could be in contention.

    Ibrahima Balde is fit again after recovering from an Achilles injury, although Souleymane Mame Faye could still be deployed in a two-man support act alongside Makengo behind striker Mamadou Kone.

    For the visitors, right-back Przemyslaw Frankowski is doubtful after leaving the Poland camp over the international break with a muscular strain.

    Rennes are, however, boosted  by the return of leading marksman Esteban Lepaul, who has netted seven times in the league and could spearhead the attack beside Boulaye Dia after shaking off an ankle concern.

    Lorient possible starting lineup:.

    Mvogo; Talbi, Adjei, Obaretin; Sylla, Avom, Cadiou, Kouassi; Faye, Makengo; Kone.

    Rennes possible starting lineup:.

    Samba; Cresswell, Ait Boudlal, Oliveira; Reynolds, Rongier, Thomasson, Szymanski, Nagida; Dia, Lepaul.

    A watertight rearguard and a fine record in this derby should leave Dujeux’s men brimming with confidence, particularly after that encouraging success on the road at Le Havre.

    However, Rennes carry far greater attacking quality, and Lepaul’s return could help them end a losing streak away from home, even if a share of the spoils looks likelier than a full haul.

    Liverpool believe a 6ft5 star might actually grow even further. He's going to be a monster.

    In a recent development, liverpool have spent the last few years amassing as much elite talent as possible. That's mainly seen in the substantial-money signings like Alexander Isak, Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola.

    Those three are all nine-figure signings and among the most expensive players in history. But it's not the only way Liverpool have gone about their plan.

    Industry observers note that they've also moved for young players. Those with elite-level talent and who require a push in the right direction to place them among the best in the world. Jeremy Jacquet might be the most obvious example in Liverpool's first-team right now.

    In a recent development, but there is another who we've been waiting to see. And Liverpool feel he hasn't even finished developing physically.

    Sources indicate that jacquet might be the star centre-back of the future right now but he wasn't a little over a year ago. Back then it was Giovanni Leoni, who arrived from Parma with incredible hype.

    However, Leoni would suffer a terrible knee injury on his debut, meaning he still hasn't actually completed 90 minutes for Liverpool. He hasn't played since, either, and only got back to training with teammates this week.

    Liverpool are managing Leoni's comeback very, very carefully. That would be the case anyway, of course, but there's an extra reason to do so here as The Times reports that the club feel he might still be growing.

    That complicates his recovery process but it also slightly surreal to hear as Leoni is already 6ft5. He's a massive defender as it is but it appears the 19-year-old may get even more massive.

    Growth like that can have negative effects. It generates extra pressure on joints, means players carry weight differently, and can lead to complications. Of course, it can also have positive effects like a player who towers over forwards and doesn't even need to jump particularly high to win headers.

    We'll see how things land with that one.

    Leoni is expected to feature at some point in the coming months. All signs suggest his rehabilitation has been good overall and Liverpool are reportedly excited about his return to the fold.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Arsenal lads were in action, and on the scoresheet, last night as England beat Spain 3-2 in Madrid.
    • Obviously I’m not especially invested in the national sides of other countries, but I was pleased for Ben White after all the nonsense he’s been through with England.
    • It has been revealed that holland was the one who sparked the issue originally when he was working with Gareth Southgate, so hopefully another goal for the Arsenal defender (he got one a few months back I think), and being part of a famous win in Spain will win around some of those fans who were giving him stick.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Arsenal lads were in action, and on the scoresheet, last night as England beat Spain 3-2 in Madrid. Ezri Konsa made it 2-0 with a close range header, Spain might wonder who was marking him (I think it was supposed to be Marc Cucurella) but the movement was really sharp. Then a couple of minute later, Ben White fired England into a 3-0 lead, with Cucurella also in close attendance.

    Obviously I’m not especially invested in the national sides of other countries, but I was pleased for Ben White after all the nonsense he’s been through with England. The worst sections of the media have fanned the flames against him, and it doesn’t take much to rile up those who are already of a jingoistic persuasion. As we’ve seen since seen with stories about Steve Holland being hugely unpopular at Man Utd, there’s a common denominator, and it’s not Ben White.

    It has been revealed that holland was the one who sparked the issue originally when he was working with Gareth Southgate, so hopefully another goal for the Arsenal defender (he got one a few months back I think), and being part of a famous win in Spain will win around some of those fans who were giving him stick. I also feel quite confident that even if there is a cohort who won’t forgive Ben White for the crime of Steve Holland being a dickhead, he probably won’t care too much. Look at the reactions of his teammates and manager to the goal, and that’s tells you plenty.

    He was also involved in a minor scuffle going off at half-time, which also seemed to involved Konsa and Martin Zubimendi, but I’m sure it was just heat of the moment stuff. Although Spain got two back after England went down to 10 men, they made the fatal mistake of starting Mikel Merino. How was he supposed to come off the bench and get a vital goal then? Silly Luis de la Fuenta, bloke’s a fraud.

    According to recent reports, elsewhere over the weekend, Viktor Gyokeres scored twice for Sweden, both from the penalty spot. We just need more penalties. This is the key to unlocking him. Riccardo Calafiori played the full 90 as Italy went down 4-1 to Belgium (ouch), Martin Odegaard played 90 as Norway beat Wales, and there are some more games to come this week with Germany facing Netherlands tonight (Kai v Timber), the Brazilians are in action in Singapore, and apparently Christos Tzolis is fit to play for Greece after having an MRI.

    According to recent reports, maybe it’s my own recent experiences, but I don’t care for the idea he needs an MRI. I get it, it’s probably for his knee or hamstring or something, but it feels like if you need one of those to know if you’re fit, you’re probably not feeling 100% anyway. I guess this will be one Mikel Arteta will keep a close eye on tonight when Greece host Serbia and Tzolis inevitably starts. Ideally, these will be useful minutes for him, and help him deliver for us but you can’t help but worry considering he picked up an injury in the last Interlull.

    Sources indicate that finally for today, it looks as if a Declan Rice contract extension is close. Speaking while on England duty, he noted:.

    “A new contract is hopefully on the horizon soon. I’m extremely lucky to be at a club like Arsenal where the manager highlights me so much trust and teammates who put so much energy and effort into to me.

    “I’m extremely lucky not to have to worry about that stuff, and it makes playing football far more easier.”.

    Industry observers note that this is, by any measure, a no-brainer. I don’t think there’s a club in the world that would turn him down if he were available, and his importance to Arsenal is just obvious. In a world when £100m+ transfers often struggle to provide value, this is one of the exceptions. If you went back to 2023 and had to do it all again, even if you added another £20m or £30m to the fee we paid West Ham, it would be worth it. It’s likely to be the kind of deal that sees him play out the rest of his prime years in red and white, and let’s hope there are more trophies along the way to accompany that.

    Right, I have to leave it there for this morning. We will have an Arsecast Extra for you a bit later on though. We’ve already put out the call for questions on BlueSky @gunnerblog.bsky.social and @arseblog.com, so fire away using the hashtag #arsecastextra – or if you’re an Arseblog Member on Patreon, leave your question in the #arsecast-extra-questions channel on our Discord server.

    In a recent development, the pod should be out around around midday. Until then, have a good one – after which I’m gonna be off for a couple of days but the lads will keep things ticking here until I get back.

    #60302. What it's really like to kill a fellow athlete - and the terrible grief 'you carry for the rest of your life': The cursed band of haunted sportsmen reveal the nightmares that never leave them

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 20m • 📚 Deep Dive (3902 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dailymail ↗ Open Full Page

    What it's really like to kill a fellow athlete - and the terrible grief 'you carry for the rest of your life': The cursed band of haunted sportsmen reveal the nightmares that never leave them

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (3902 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dailymail

    ⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Published: 21:00 EST, 19 November 2026 | Updated: 22:15 EST, 19 November 2026.
    • Towards the end of the Australian summer of 2014-15, as the country prepared to host the Cricket World Cup, I took a flight from Sydney to Hobart, Tasmania, to watch a Sheffield Shield game between Tasmania and New South Wales at the Bellerive Oval, a beautiful ground perched on the banks of the Derwent River.
    • In a recent development, australian sport was still in shock.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By OLIVER HOLT, CHIEF SPORTS WRITER.

    Published: 21:00 EST, 19 November 2026 | Updated: 22:15 EST, 19 November 2026.

    Towards the end of the Australian summer of 2014-15, as the country prepared to host the Cricket World Cup, I took a flight from Sydney to Hobart, Tasmania, to watch a Sheffield Shield game between Tasmania and New South Wales at the Bellerive Oval, a beautiful ground perched on the banks of the Derwent River.

    In a recent development, australian sport was still in shock. A few months earlier, Australia's Test opener, Phillip Hughes, had died after he was struck on the side of his neck by a short ball from a young bowler called Sean Abbott in a game between Newly introduced South Wales and South Australia at the Sydney Cricket Ground.

    Recent findings suggest that hughes was treated at the ground for 40 minutes and then taken by ambulance to St Vincent's Hospital in nearby Darlinghurst in a critical condition. 'Feeling for Phil Hughes after being hit,' former Australia Test cricketer Dean Jones wrote on Twitter. 'He is not in a good way! Stay strong Sean Abbott. Not your fault, young man.'.

    The impact of the ball had compressed a vein in Hughes' neck and when it split, it caused a catastrophic bleed on the brain. Hughes had emergency surgery and was placed in an induced coma. He never regained consciousness and passed away two days later.

    Sources indicate that hughes was a popular, talented, gutsy cricketer with three Test centuries already under his belt. A small guy with the heart of a lion. He was 25 years old. Cricket mourned a terrible tragedy – some called it the sport's saddest day and the agony of Hughes' family was hard to bear. But there was something else. There was an awareness that two tragedies were playing out in front of us.

    Recent findings suggest that hughes was lost but the man who had bowled the delivery that felled him had been left behind, desolate and distraught. Many thought Sean Abbott, who was 22, would never play cricket again. That he would not be able to find the strength. But that was why I had flown to Tasmania. Because Abbott had found the strength.

    Phil Hughes was the golden boy of Australian cricket in 2014, with three Test centuries already to his name, when he was hit by a ball bowled by Sean Abbott and died.

    Abbott visiting the Sydney hospital where Hughes was in a coma that he would never wake from, having suffered a catastrophic bleed on the brain.

    Sources indicate that that February afternoon at the Bellerive Oval, I sat among a smattering of spectators who watched Abbott walk to the top of his mark. His team-mates shouted encouragement to him. They were willing him on with everything they had and Abbott bowled his heart out.

    Sources indicate that 'Beautifully bowled, Abbo,' one of the NSW fielders shouted after one ball to former Test opener Ed Cowan. 'That's a beauty, Seanie,' another yelled after the fifth ball of his first over, when Cowan jerked his head out of the way of a short delivery so fast he fell over. Only one wicket fell that afternoon. Abbott took it.

    According to recent reports, it was one of the bravest sporting performances I have ever witnessed. Because even though cricket had voiced its support for Abbott, the sport could not protect him from his thoughts and from the knowledge he had become one of a cursed band of sportsmen who have unwittingly caused the death of an opponent during a contest.

    It has been revealed that sometimes, tragedy in sport is not just the tragedy of the player who dies; it is the tragedy of the opponent who must live the nightmare of what he has done over and over again in his mind. To those that it has befallen, they say it is a grief that never leaves them.

    Sources indicate that that grief, that sense of a double tragedy, was brought sharply back into focus earlier this month when Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel died in hospital the day after a sickening collision with FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono. The accident happened in the final minutes of a game in Spain's Segunda Division, when Owono hurtled out of his goal and collided with De Miguel in the centre circle. He was shown a red card for the foul.

    According to recent reports, there was an outpouring of grief for De Miguel. I was among those who observed a minute's silence for him before the Barcelona-Aston Villa Champions League tie at the Nou Camp the next evening. Tributes continue to be paid to him. Owono, meanwhile, has become a pariah. It is stated that the 25-year-old rarely leaves his house.

    According to recent reports, owono does not appear to have had the same sympathy extended to him that Abbott benefited from. His challenge on De Miguel, a striker who had had a peripatetic career in Spain's lower leagues, was reckless and cavalier. For him, the struggle with guilt and responsibility and public judgment is only just beginning.

    FC Andorra will play their first home game since the tragedy against Leganes on Friday night but when they run out at the Encamp Stadium, a neat little ground beside a babbling river, the Valira d'Orient, and in the shadow of the mountains that make Andorra such a popular ski resort, Owono will not be there.

    Earlier this month Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel died in hospital the day after a sickening collision with FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono.

    It has been revealed that owono has become a pariah. It is mentioned that the 25-year-old rarely leaves his house.

    The goalkeeper, who has 47 caps for Equatorial Guinea, was given the maximum sentence of a 12-match ban by the Spanish Football Federation.

    Tenerife manager Alvaro Cervera suggested Owono's ban 'might feel light' to all those mourning the striker, who was 30 years old, while FC Andorra owner Gerard Pique, the former Barcelona and Spain centre back, remarked the maximum sanction 'puts him (Owono) in a situation he does not deserve, because he is not to blame for all of this having happened'.

    No one knows whether Owono will feel able to return to football when his ban ends. Footage circulated of him in an on-field argument moments before the clash with De Miguel, and it was used to suggest that he was in an unstable state of mind.

    In a recent development, some have pressed for him to be charged with manslaughter. His Instagram account was deactivated after it was deluged with abuse, including messages which branded him 'a murderer'. It has been reported that his brother, who is also a footballer, has been the victim of abuse because of his association with Owono.

    It has been revealed that owono has only communicated through a statement released by his club. 'These are the most difficult days of my life,' he wrote. 'I struggle to find the words, and I find it very hard to ​process what has happened. I feel enormous pain at the loss of Jesus. I think of him, his family, and all the people who loved him. I know there will be many questions to address, and I will face whatever comes with the utmost respect.'.

    I spoke to the great British fighter Barry McGuigan about Owono this week. McGuigan has suffered his share of tragedies. His brother, Dermot, took his own life. He lost his daughter, Danika, to cancer when she was just 33, in 2019. And in 1982, three years before he won the world featherweight title at Loftus Road, he nearly quit boxing altogether.

    In the 12th fight of his professional career, McGuigan fought a Nigerian boxer called Young Ali at the World Sporting Club in Mayfair. He still remembers the clink of cutlery coming from the diners who were sitting ringside that night. That sound still takes him back.

    McGuigan still remembers the sequence of punches that put Young Ali down in the sixth round of the fight. He saw his opponent's eyes roll back in his head and a feeling of dread washed over him. Young Ali, just 21, fell into a coma from which he never emerged and died five months later.

    I spoke to the great British fighter Barry McGuigan (right) about Owono this week. McGuigan has suffered his share of tragedies.

    'There was the horror of that and we sat and we waited and we prayed that he would be better and he never got better,' McGuigan told me. 'I didn't know whether I wanted to continue boxing. I thought: "If I can do this to somebody…"'.

    He shuddered when he talked about Owono. 'Other tragedies happen and other terrible things happen,' he remarked. 'Life is a struggle. Something like that, you never leave it behind you.

    'It is something invisible and it depends how emotionally vulnerable he is. He may never be the same again but I hope he is able to overcome it.'.

    There are others out there in sport, still trying to overcome it. Think of Matt Petgrave, the Sheffield Steelers ice-hockey player who was arrested on suspicion of manslaughter after his skate fatally cut the neck of Nottingham Panthers' Adam Johnson in an Elite Ice Hockey League match at Sheffield Arena in October 2023.

    In a recent development, think of Jochen Mass, the Formula One driver, who spent years blaming himself for the death of Gilles Villeneuve during qualifying for the Belgian Grand Prix at Zolder in 1982, because he slowed and moved to the right in front of Villeneuve. The Ferrari ran into the back of Mass and flipped in grotesque cartwheels across the track.

    Think of Matthias Behr, the German fencer who killed his opponent, Vladimir Smirnov, at the 1982 World Fencing Championships in Rome when Behr's foil blade broke during a match, penetrated the Ukrainian fencer's mask and pierced his eye.

    Think of Gary Cully, the Irish fighter, who learned this week that his last opponent, Lee Reeves, had died after spending three months in a coma following their bout in Dublin in August.

    'What a character and a gent,' Cully wrote in tribute to Reeves. 'It's never been nothing but love between us champ, can't really believe I'm writing this but RIP brother.'.

    Nottingham Panthers' Adam Johnson died in October 2023 when opponent Matt Petgrave's skate cut his neck during a match.

    Gary Cully (left), the Irish fighter, learned this week that his last opponent, Lee Reeves (right), had died after spending three months in a coma following their bout in Dublin in August.

    Dr Victor Thompson, a prominent UK clinical sports psychologist, has studied the effect on competitors of being involved in the death of a rival.

    It has been revealed that 'The biggest thing a player will have had to absorb normally is bad performance,' Dr Thompson says. 'Now he has to absorb the fact that he was involved in somebody dying. He will be trying to work out was it his fault? Is he to blame? And all of that, because the emotions are so high, gets associated with playing the sport in question.

    'So when Sean Abbott thought about going out there again, when he thought about putting his pads on, or putting his kit on and being around team-mates or the smell of the cricket bat – it'll all be associated to that very traumatic day.'.

    It has been revealed that university of North Carolina academic John M Silva III argued that aggression in sport is defined in two categories: hostile aggression and instrumental aggression. Hostile is when the main aim is to cause harm or injury to your opponent. Instrumental is aggression for a purpose, perhaps ball recovery or to sow doubt in an opponent’s mind.

    The interpretation of a player's actions at a time of high stress, frustration or adversarial combat is often central to the reaction to a sporting tragedy. Whether forgiveness is extended to or opprobrium visited on the competitor who has caused the death of another.

    Sources indicate that that interpretation was used against Petgrave, who was notorious for having a bad disciplinary record on the ice. Some likened the action which fatally injured Johnson to a kung-fu kick and drew a link between it and some of his past behaviour. He was mercilessly trolled on social media. Team-mates, and many ice hockey fans, leapt to his defence and remarked any suggestion his action was deliberate was fanciful. They said his unusual action in lifting his left skate high was a direct result of being knocked off balance by a collision.

    In a recent development, petgrave could not return to ice hockey immediately even if he had wanted to. It was a full 18 months before the Crown Prosecution Service and South Yorkshire Police decided there was no realistic prospect of conviction for manslaughter and that no criminal charges should be brought against the 34-year-old Canadian.

    In the intervening period, Petgrave's family set up a crowdfunding page, pointing out that he was unable to work or to return home until the CPS had decided whether to press charges. The page raised nearly £20,000 from well-wishers.

    The interpretation of a player's actions at a time of high stress, frustration or adversarial combat is often central to the reaction to a sporting tragedy - as it was for Petgrave.

    Petgrave did receive widespread support from inside his sport, with a standing ovation at his Sheffield side's next home match, while he was beginning 18 months under investigation.

    'This has been the most painful and overwhelming period of our lives,' a message from Petgrave's family said at the bottom of the page. 'Watching someone I love go through this has been incredibly difficult.

    It has been revealed that 'Despite everything, we are doing our best to stay strong, and the support and kindness from so many people have been a source of strength. We continue to recognise the heartbreaking nature of this situation, and our thoughts remain with everyone affected. We hold on to hope that this will soon come to an end.'.

    In a recent development, petgrave now plies his trade in the minor league ECHL for the Indy Fuel, a team based in Fishers, Indiana. He is an ever-present this season, playing opponents like the Wheeling Nailers, the Greenville Swamp Rabbits, the Kalamazoo Wings and the Bloomington Bison.

    It has been revealed that 'We understand the responsibility that comes with the great support we receive from this community,' Sean Hallett, CEO of Hallett Sports, which owns the Fuel, noted when they hired Petgrave. 'We are confident he will be a positive addition to our team and our city.'.

    According to recent reports, I wrote to the Fuel, asking if there was any chance of speaking to Petgrave. They did not respond. The reticence is understandable and, in many ways, laudable. Players involved in this kind of tragedy are preoccupied with respect for the victims' families and the sensitivities that come with such terrible grief. There is nothing they can say or do to make it better.

    It has been revealed that sometimes, it is the other way round. Sometimes, it is the family of a lost loved one who find a way to ease the pain of a sportsman eaten up by shame for inadvertently causing the death of a competitor.

    Mass, who died last year, blamed himself for the sickening crash that killed the most exciting, charismatic, talented, electrifying driver in Formula One. As Villeneuve's Ferrari cartwheeled across the track, breaking into pieces, he was flung clear of the wreckage still strapped to his seat, catapulting across the track until he came to rest in the catch-fencing by the side of the circuit. He died of catastrophic injuries later that evening, aged 32.

    In a recent development, mass was absolved of responsibility. It was a tragic accident. Villeneuve was running hot after a disagreement with his team-mate Didier Pironi and was pushing even his own boundaries. There were any number of extenuating circumstances but Mass still blamed himself. He retired from the sport the same season.

    As Gilles Villeneuve's Ferrari cartwheeled across the track, breaking into pieces, he was flung clear of the wreckage still strapped to his seat, catapulting across the track.

    Despite being absolved of responsibility, Jochen Mass (pictured in 2019) blamed himself for the accident and retired from the sport the same year.

    It was years later when he felt a tap on the shoulder as he was sitting on a plane. He looked up to see Villeneuve's son, Jacques, the 1997 F1 world champion, standing over him.

    Sources indicate that 'I felt so guilty about what had happened and then suddenly, there was Jacques,' Mass recalled. 'He said: "Jochen, our family – we never blamed you. It was a racing incident – just a wrong decision by the two of you."'.

    All the shame that Mass felt ebbed away. He found his own peace just as Behr found redemption by sheltering the grandchildren of Smirnov and his widow, Emma, at his home in Germany to protect them from the Russian invasion of Ukraine.

    It has been revealed that behr, tortured by guilt about the accident that killed Smirnov, had written to Emma 30 years ago but the letter was lost. When he did not receive a reply, he was convinced that Smirnov's widow blamed him for killing her husband.

    Sources indicate that they finally met when a television documentary crew brought them together and Emma reassured Behr that she had never held him responsible. Behr has suffered from depression and suicidal thoughts because of flashbacks to the fatal accident.

    According to recent reports, 'They are always there,' Behr said later. 'Even if I go into a liquor store and see vodka with the Smirnoff label on it, the thoughts of what happened immediately come back to me. But now that I am playing a part in the lives of Vladimir's grandchildren, it has come full circle for me. It was a gift for me. I can finally give something back.'.

    In a recent development, maybe Abbott has been trying to give something back all these years, too. Perhaps the fine career he has had is his tribute to Hughes. He has represented Australia in one-day and Twenty20 cricket and is the all-time leading wicket-taker in the Substantial Bash League. He has represented Surrey in English cricket and was part of Australia's World Cup winning squad in 2023.

    Recent findings suggest that many had worried that Abbott would not play again after Hughes' death. Not your fault, young man. Easy to say, harder to grasp amid the grief and the disbelief. But there was an outpouring of support for him, including from Hughes' family.

    Perhaps the fine career 2023 World Cup winner Sean Abbott (bottom right) has had is his tribute to Hughes.

    That afternoon at the Bellerive Oval, I asked him about the day's play as he came off. He mentioned he was happy with how it had gone. Afterwards, I sat in the stand with Abbott's team-mate Nathan Lyon, the Australia spinner, who spoke movingly about Hughes and about Abbott. At the end of the interview I thanked him for making the time to speak to me in such difficult circumstances. 'Too easy, mate,' he said.

    Except it wasn't too easy. Inside, Lyon and the rest of Australian cricket were still in agony. Later that day, Lyon complained to Cricket Australia that he had not been expecting to be asked about Hughes. He was upset about my questions. I had made a misjudgment. Things were still too raw.

    Sources indicate that lyon was comfortable talking about Abbott, though. 'The way Sean has carried himself through the whole incident, well, credit goes to him,' Lyon said. 'He is a very impressive bloke. I've got a lot of time for him. He will do anything to help anyone out. He always puts mates first. He always has your back. He is a typical good mate. I'm proud to call him a mate.

    'I think (Abbott not playing again) went through the minds of a few of us. But natural instinct will come over and you do what you do best and if that's play cricket, you go out and play cricket. It's about being around your mates and the mates who are there with him now, they're the guys who are going to get him through it.'.

    Abbott has never spoken about the tragedy. He gave written evidence in January 2016 to the inquest into Hughes' death.

    'I saw him start to sway and I ran to the other end of the pitch and I held the right side of his head with my left hand,' Abbott wrote. 'I remained on the field until Phillip was placed on the medicab and then returned to the changing room. Once in the changing room I felt confused and upset, I had a headache, people kept coming up to me but I cannot recall what they remarked.'.

    In a recent development, much of the inquest was dominated by suggestions that Hughes had been subjected to a barrage of short balls and sledging. The inquest heard that Abbott's bowling partner, Doug Bollinger, had noted to Hughes 'I'm going to kill you' at one stage during the game. Bollinger denied that accusation. Abbott was exonerated of any responsibility for the tragedy that unfolded.

    Only rarely are there glimpses of the impact that Hughes' death has had on him. At a tribute to Hughes on the tenth anniversary of his death, Abbott broke down and wept at the end of the minute's silence at the SCG. One of his team-mates put an arm around his shoulders to try to comfort him.

    Abbott at Hughes' funeral in his hometown of Macksville, Australia, in 2014.

    'The difficulty with boxing is that you are in this sport to hurt your opponent,' notes McGuigan. 'Nobody believes - or wants to believe - that it is going to do lasting damage'.

    In a recent development, mcGuigan says the pain never quite goes away. 'I had a love-hate relationship with boxing,' he says. 'The difficulty with boxing is that you are in this sport to hurt your opponent. Nobody believes – or wants to believe – that it is going to do lasting damage.

    It has been revealed that yesterday, Luka returned to Milanello and trained with the Rossoneri, ready to take charge of the group again when the tournament resumes.     📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Lewis Nolan | 20 Nov 2026 18:34, Last updated: 20 Nov 2026 19:54.

    Augsburg's WWK Arena will be the backdrop for their clash with Mainz 05 on Sunday in a potentially pivotal clash in the battle against relegation.

    The home side are 14th in the Bundesliga table with nine points, whereas their opponents are 12th with 10, and a loss for either could leave them in the bottom three.

    Augsburg are only two points above 16th-placed Union Berlin, who occupy the relegation playoff spot, while they are just three points ahead of 17th-placed Schalke 04.

    The hosts are winless in their past seven league matches, a period in which they claimed just three points and suffered four defeats.

    Head coach Manuel Baum will not be pleased that his team conceded at least two goals in six of those fixtures, though he will highlight that the club netted 13 times in that stretch.

    Fuggerstadter have played five contests at WWK Arena in 2026-27, and they have triumphed once, drawn three times and won once at the stadium.

    Two of those stalemates came against Bayern Munich and Bayer Leverkusen, while their only defeat at home came against third-placed Freiburg at the end of October.

    The visitors come into the clash looking to avoid a fifth consecutive loss in all competitions, and avoid losing a fourth straight Bundesliga game.

    Perhaps the saving grace for Mainz is that the rest of the bottom seven play teams right now in the top eight, meaning it is unlikely that they will end the weekend in the relegation zone.

    Urs Fischer's side did score four goals in their four losses, but they conceded on 11 occasions, and their latest defeat saw them ship twice when they lost 2-1 against Bayern Munich on November 7.

    Mainz's record on the road has been largely positive this term, as while they were beaten 4-1 by Elversberg on October 30, they did emerge as winners in their first three away Bundesliga outings of the campaign.

    The club are also unbeaten in their five most recent meetings with Augsburg, claiming victory four times, including when they won 2-0 in February.

    Augsburg form (all competitions):.

    Mainz 05 form (all competitions):.

    Augsburg only have two confirmed absentees, with Han-Noah Massengo and defender Chrislain Matsima ruled out.

    Juma Bah, Jeffrey Gouweleeuw and Yannik Keitel could be trusted together in defence, while Robin Fellhauer and Fabian Rieder may start in a double pivot.

    Striker Michael Gregoritsch has scored five times in the league this season, and he is certain to lead the line, supported by Anton Kade and Alexis Claude-Maurice.

    Though Mainz only have to contend with the absence of centre-back Dominik Kohr, he is not scheduled to return until January because of an ankle injury.

    Stefan Posch, Fabio Gruber and Kacper Potulski are likely candidates to start in the team's back three, and the trio may be protected by Paul Nebel and Kaishu Sano from midfield.

    Augsburg possible starting lineup:.

    Dahmen; Bah, Gouweleeuw, Keitel; Wolf, Fellhauer, Rieder, Behrens; Kade, Claude-Maurice; Gregoritsch.

    Mainz 05 possible starting lineup:.

    Zentner; Posch, Gruber, Potulski; Caci, Nebel, Sano, Amiri, Mwene; Tietz, Becker.

    Neither Augsburg nor Mainz have been particularly strong defensively, so it would be surprising if either kept a clean sheet.

    The hosts boast the advantage of playing at WWK Arena, but the visitors have often travelled well, and the two may ultimately have to settle for a point on Sunday.

    • According to recent reports, it’s Andrew A covering for Andrew M, who’s playing hooky again.
