    • Sources indicate that it’s either that or tears, and my eye juice reserves are running low after reading just a fraction of the thousands of messages you sent over the weekend.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, it’s Andrew A covering for Andrew M, who’s playing hooky again. I suppose after 24 years of writing this blog, a few bad habits are bound to creep in….

    Sources indicate that I’m not going to lie, it’s been a difficult week. Fortunately, a lifetime of watching Arsenal has given me plenty of practice at making bad jokes when I don’t know what else to say.

    Sources indicate that it’s either that or tears, and my eye juice reserves are running low after reading just a fraction of the thousands of messages you sent over the weekend. Bluesky, Reddit, X, Discord, Facebook, Patreon. Wherever I looked, there you were, sending love to Blogs. It was beautiful to see.

    In a recent development, and to the handful of you who got in touch with me or people I know because you thought Friday’s enhancement was about my health, please hold that thought. I’m fine. Touch wood. There are, in fact, two Andrews at Arseblog, and I’m the other one.

    Having been crowned the “World’s Youngest Boy” by James on yesterday’s Arsecast Extra, Max Dowman set yet another record last night, becoming England under-21s’ youngest scorer with the winner in a 3-2 victory over France in filthy conditions in Bristol.

    Recent findings suggest that I’d planned to watch from kick-off, but gave up when I realised the game wasn’t on any of the 5,000 channels I pay £150 a month for. Then I saw on social media that Ethan Nwaneri, playing as a number 10, had laid on a couple of goals. So I did the clever thing and googled it. Turns out I needed the official England app and an account. Eyes still rolling, I tried to set up a login, only to find out I already had one. Cue the password reset process, verification codes and me losing the will to live. Just let me watch some fucking children play football in the rain!

    By the time I got the stream, it was nearly half-time. At least that gave me a chance to catch up on Nwaneri’s two assists, both of which were Ozil-esque. First he drove down the left and slipped a neat ball inside for Mikey Moore, currently on loan at Cologne, to finish. Then came a teasing dink to the back post that Southampton’s Divin Mubama met first time. Given how little Nwaneri has played for Dortmund lately, it was a welcome reminder of what he can do.

    It feels a bit silly to say Max, who was named player of the match, looked comfortable at this level when he’s already got a Premier League winners’ medal next to his GCSE textbooks, but he really did.

    Sources indicate that watching him is like reading someone’s really nice handwriting. Even the everyday stuff looks lovely. A touch to bring the ball under control, a little turn, and suddenly the defender who was right up his arse is looking at the back of his shirt. I’ll never get tired of watching him do that.

    In a recent development, as both sides made changes, I expected Lee Carsley to take him off. Instead, he played the full 90 and dug Arsenal teammate Tommy Setford out of a hole. The goalkeeper was at fault for the only goal in Friday’s defeat to Portugal and had another difficult night, spilling a cross into his own net. The rain hardly helped, and the 20-year-old has been doing well on loan at Stevenage, but it was a horrible one to concede.

    When Brest’s Giovani Versini whipped in an equaliser with five minutes left, it looked like England would have to settle for a draw, but Dowman’s tap-in settled it with a minute to spare. Who knows, Dowman and Nwaneri could be on the same pitch again next week when Dortmund visit the Emirates.

    Elsewhere, Group 2 of League A of the UEFA Nations League (catchy naming scheme, lads) served up another bonkers evening. Jurrien Timber scored twice in the Netherlands’ 7-0 win over Christos Tzolis’ Greece on Friday, only for the Dutch to lose 5-0 to Kai Havertz’s Germany in Berlin. There were some lovely goals from the Germans – including two from Florian Wirtz – who are finding their feet under Jurgen Klopp. Timber and Havertz both came off midway through the second half, seemingly unscathed. Timber’s pride aside, anyway.

    Tzolis, meanwhile, was cleared to play after an MRI scan and got through 88 minutes of Greece’s 1-0 win over Serbia. All three sides finished on 11 points, with Germany and the Netherlands going through on goal difference at Greece’s expense.

    Sources indicate that tonight, Martin Odegaard’s Norway face Denmark, while Viktor Gyokeres will look to extend his record-breaking scoring run for Sweden away at Poland. Piero Hincapie’s Ecuador take on Bolivia, Big Gabi and Bruno are in Singapore with Brazil, and Cristhian Mosquera and Marli Salmon are in action for Spain under-21s and England under-19s, respectively.

    According to recent reports, closer to home, The Athletic ran two Arsenal contract stories in quick succession. James reports that Timber has agreed a fresh long-term deal, while David Ornstein says Declan Rice’s extension will take him through to 2031. Arsenal already had the option to keep Rice until 2029, so the new deal effectively buys them two more years and gives him a sizeable pay rise for the next four and a half. If he keeps playing as he has been, I can’t imagine many Arsenal fans quibbling with that.

    For what it’s worth, we’ve heard on the grapevine that David Raya’s fresh contract is all but done, too, which means the club are making good progress with the lads whose deals expire in 2028, a list that also includes Odegaard, Havertz, Mikel Merino and our two backup keepers.

    There was an interesting discussion on Arsenal Vision’s ‘Friday Night Clive’ podcast about Arsenal elongating their “winning window” while having one eye on the next iteration of the team. If you hand expensive newly introduced contracts to players hurtling towards their thirties, you leave yourself financially exposed and potentially blocking pathways for up-and-coming talent. No doubt the club and manager are keenly aware of that. I just wonder how much you can expect the latter to focus on the faraway future when the dynasty he craves has to start in the here and now.

    Sources indicate that if this week has taught me anything, it’s that there’s something to be mentioned for seizing the day. Admittedly, that’s easier when it’s Arsenal’s money I’m volunteering to spend.

    If you’re about to part with some of your own (smooth segue, Allen) this year’s Arseblog Christmas Gift Guide is up.

    Recent findings suggest that I spent some of last week rounding up Arsenal bits and pieces I’d be happy to find under the tree. Mostly, I wanted to point you towards the independent makers, artists and writers producing stuff I like. In many cases, what I’ve picked is just a small sample of what they do, so have a nose around.

    If you’ve got a recommendation of your own, pop the link in the form at the bottom and I’ll take a look.

    Right, I’d better crack on with the day job. Lewis is on duty tomorrow and, all being well, Andrew M should be back here before the week is out.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Good morning! I’ve got to say, if I worked at Arsenal and I wasn’t getting a fresh contract this international break, I think I’d be taking it pretty personally.

    After Monday’s news that both Jurrien Timber and Declan Rice have agreed latest deals with the club, Tuesday brought the news that fellow 2023 signing David Raya was next in line, swiftly followed by reports that Riccardo Calafiori will also be handed a new deal, and Piero Hincapie will be getting improved terms, too.

    According to recent reports, since the end of the 2024-25 season, there have already been new deals for Gabriel, Myles Lewis-Skelly, Ethan Nwaneri, William Saliba, Bukayo Saka, and, of course, Mikel Arteta. With the latest raft of agreements on top of those, that’s a lot of key people tied down for the next few years.

    These deals will mean everyone other than Kai Havertz, Martin Odegaard, Ben White, Mikel Merino, and Kepa is contracted to the club until at least 2029. That’s a nice feeling, isn’t it? There will be some decisions to be made over a couple of those players and whether it’s time to refresh, you’d imagine, but the bulk of the squad should be staying put and continuing to compete together – with a couple of additions supplementing them, of course – for the next couple of years at least.

    Of those four (plus Kepa) mentioned above, you’d have to think Odegaard is the next priority when it comes to renewals, given his importance on and off the pitch and his current form.

    In a recent development, I was in a bar here in Berlin catching up with a fellow Arsenal fan yesterday evening (hello, if you’re reading!) and they had Norway’s game in Denmark on. It’s fair to say the skipper continued his fine start to the season.

    According to recent reports, after Norway went two down against the run of play, Odegaard sprung into action. No player had as many touches on the night, and he was involved in all three Norway goals.

    He stole the ball for the goal that made it 2-1, which, by the way, we should have a word for. We have the word equaliser for when it goes to 2-2, but we don’t have a word for the goal that shortens the lead. The Germans call it an Anschlusstor – literally a ‘connecting goal’, the goal that means the scores are now just one apart.

    Anyway, Odegaard, pressing as he always does, stole the ball from goalkeeper Mads Hermansen, then selflessly left the tap-in for Erling Haaland. He then scored the equaliser, a goal reminiscent of his opening day strike against Coventry if we’re honest: he didn’t hit it well, he got a bit lucky. But: right place, right time and all that.

    And, finally, it was Odegaard’s ferociously whipped in free-kick that struck the hand of Joachim Andersen and allowed Haaland to convert from the penalty spot late into added time. If you’ve got a few minutes, you can see the highlights of his performance here – some of the touches are more than worth your time.

    A good night’s work, especially after he was suffering with a stomach bug last week.

    It wasn’t just the captain in action yesterday, either. Piero Hincapie played just over an hour for Ecuador overnight, there were assists for Gabriel and Bruno Guimaraes as Brazil beat Singapore 7-0 earlier on in the day, and then an assist for Viktor Gyokeres too as Sweden drew with Poland.

    That looks like something he’s clearly worked on – getting his body in the way of the defender and, rather than holding the ball up, looking to direct it towards an oncoming runner. His assist for Declan Rice in Munich obviously looked pretty similar, and it’s not something we saw too much of last season.

    It has been revealed that in fact, I thought I’d have a quick look, and Gyokeres has 13 key passes (a pass that leads a shot from a team-mate) in the Premier League and Champions League this season. He’s delivering a key pass every 28.4 minutes. Last season he had a key pass every 104 minutes across those two competitions. It’s hard not to conclude that he’s been working on that side of his game, and these Giroud-esque back-to-goal touches for team-mates are more than welcome.

    In a recent development, so, plenty of assists this break. Now we just need to harness that at Newcastle on Saturday and actually have someone to stick the ball in the back of the net at the end of those moves. Thankfully – knock on wood – it seems the players have made it through the break unscathed (there was also another behind-closed-doors appearance for William Saliba – a nod to Tom Canton for that story) and should be raring to go.

    It has been revealed that lastly, I want to point you towards Arseblog News, where Andrew A wrote something last night on the death of double-winner Peter Storey, one of just eight players to make over 500 appearances for the club. That first double is such an enormous part of our history wouldn’t have happened without Storey’s nerves of steel in the FA Cup semi-final.

    Report: Liverpool given alternative solution to sign £33m sensation ahead of Man United

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (567 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • If they don't, they'll be left behind by their rivals and will probably end up falling even further down the Premier League table than they right now find themselves.
    • Of course, being fourth in the league isn't the end of the world but, considering the fact that they've spent over £600 million on fresh players across the last couple of seasons, you'd have expected a lot more from them.
    • The nine points that separate first-place Arsenal and Liverpool needs to get chopped down so that they can start their charge for the Premier League title.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Liverpool need to make some transfers in January.

    If they don't, they'll be left behind by their rivals and will probably end up falling even further down the Premier League table than they right now find themselves.

    Of course, being fourth in the league isn't the end of the world but, considering the fact that they've spent over £600 million on fresh players across the last couple of seasons, you'd have expected a lot more from them.

    The nine points that separate first-place Arsenal and Liverpool needs to get chopped down so that they can start their charge for the Premier League title.

    The easiest way for them to do this is going to be adding fresh players to their ranks and, with the next transfer window now just a month and a half away, deals need to start being put in place.

    Liverpool could sign Alejandro Balde on loan with an option to buy.

    Left-back has recently become a major issue for Liverpool.

    Most fans thought that, when Milos Kerkez was brought in, the left-back would quickly become Liverpool's first-choice.

    And, while Arne Slot tried to give him that, it was clear that he wasn't quite ready for the step up from Bournemouth.

    This led to Andy Robertson being given a more prominent role again and, since he's now gone, questions have been asked about their left-back.

    Kostas Tsimikas is another option that Liverpool have at their disposal but, the fact that TEAMtalk are now reporting that Alejandro Balde could be on his way to Anfield is excellent news.

    "Liverpool and Manchester United have been informed of the deal Barcelona are prepared to accept for Alejandro Balde, with the Spanish giants ready to sanction his departure in January," they wrote.

    "TEAMtalk can confirm that Balde’s agent, Jorge Mendes, has held discussions with both Liverpool and Manchester United, with the two Premier League giants having been made aware of the conditions surrounding a potential deal.

    "Both clubs are actively looking at left-back additions ahead of January and view the Barcelona defender as an attractive option.

    "TEAMtalk understands that Mendes has communicated a valuation of €40million (£33m) to interested clubs.

    "That figure would apply whether the deal is structured as a permanent transfer or a loan arrangement with an option to buy.".

    Alejandro Balde would help solve two of Liverpool's problems.

    As mentioned, left-back is one of Liverpool's main problems right now.

    However, there are other areas among their ranks which are also struggling.

    Midfield is probably the main area that fans will feel like they need to upgrade.

    Alexis Mac Allister and Trey Nyoni are their two best options right now and, even though both Dominik Szoboszlai and Ryan Gravenberch can also cover those positions, each of them have proven that they can barely play in a double pivot.

    According to recent reports, however, alongside both of these positions, right back is also an issue. Ronald Araujo may be leaving and, with the injury history that Conor Bradley and Jeremie Frimpong have, it's unclear whether they'll be reliable enough for Liverpool to trust.

    Right now, the £33 million for Balde may feel like a lot of money but, if Araujo isn't signed, Tsimkas leaves and both Frimpong and Bradley end up side-lined, Liverpool are going to be so weak at the back.

    Here's hoping that the changes they need to make get done.

    Manchester United are like John Toshack’s duvet. You fix one problem – being far too vulnerable to conceding goals – only to create another – lacking the threat to score. It is all very Meh United not Man United. The indisputable fact is they are just not very entertaining to watch. They are slow and dull.

    In a recent development, in the end it also points to another thing. The thing highlighted in midweek by Lisandro Martínez after the Champions League defeat at Atlético Madrid: they do not have the strength in depth to compete.

    Industry observers note that what they do have appears to not be fit for purpose. Certainly Michael Carrick, the under-pressure manager, is struggling to get the best out of the resources he has.

    “It’s like a duvet,” Toshack, the former Real Madrid and Wales manager, famously noted of football. “If you pull it up, your feet get cold. If you pull it down, your shoulders get cold.”.

    There will have been times in the last few days, with the intense criticism and scrutiny over his future, when Carrick will have simply felt like dragging that duvet up over his head and keeping it there.

    In a recent development, defeat by Leeds United would have been unthinkable. It would have put Carrick under potentially intolerable pressure in what appears to be a pivotal week, with Como away in the Champions League and a home Premier League fixture against Bournemouth in the coming days.

    In a recent development, was this a lifeline or the tightening of the noose for Carrick? Time will soon tell. The relief of avoiding defeat was tempered by the reality of it now being just one win in their opening seven league games – at home to newly promoted Ipswich Town – and they are down in 13th place. It is six games without a win in all competitions.

    In a recent development, that is unacceptable and is their fewest number of league victories in a top-flight campaign since 1986-87. Back then they sacked their manager in November and brought in a certain Alex Ferguson.

    Recent findings suggest that the hard truth is Carrick needs to start collecting some “Ws” in those results columns. United are already 14 points behind leaders Manchester City and five outside the probable Champions League places. Qualifying again for that tournament must be the minimum expectation.

    Ruben Amorim, Carrick’s predecessor, lost his job within 24 hours of the same 1-1 scoreline at Elland Road last season – dismissed after Martínez-like explosive comments again aimed at director of football Jason Wilcox. Carrick will not suffer the same fate after this, but the ice is becoming increasingly thin.

    It has been revealed that we have seen this movie before at United. A slow start to the season, a period of drift, falling out of contention, no reaction on the pitch, backing from the hierarchy that becomes increasingly unconvincing. And then a change.

    Can Carrick, who genuinely does still retain support at the highest level, alter that pattern? Does he have it in him? Is he too passive like his team? Carrick stated this draw felt like a “fresh start”, but on this evidence that comment can be classified as wildly optimistic.

    Sources indicate that having directed his criticism at the United hierarchy, and specifically Wilcox, the former Leeds winger who was here, over a lack of summer signings, Martínez apologised and was named in the starting XI. But the Argentine only lasted to half-time, withdrawn injured with a tight thigh, and sat watching the second half with his hood up over his head.

    What United did sign in the last window was three midfielders – at a cost of £155m – and all three started: Carlos Baleba alongside Andrey Santos with Youri Tielemans in the No 10 role, which meant Bruno Fernandes was pushed out to the left, from where he constantly wanted to come in-field, with Amad Diallo on the right.

    Industry observers note that carrick talked of having a “fresh spine” as well as that fresh start. But it did not make for a potent combination even if, further forward, Bryan Mbeumo played through the middle and scored one. He should have scored another.

    Gyok stats, KMI nonsense, wrong Bournemouth player linked

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that andrew M here after a couple of days ‘off’, but not the kind where you sit in a hammock and have delicious things brought to you.
    • The Interlull is over and that’s it now until March.
    • I was quite interested in Lewis’ quick look at Viktor Gyokeres and his key pass metrics from yesterday’s blog: He’s delivering a key pass every 28.4 minutes.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that andrew M here after a couple of days ‘off’, but not the kind where you sit in a hammock and have delicious things brought to you. More the kind where you have three stab wounds in your abdomen and a chunk of your insides taken out. If at all possible, I seriously recommend the former to the latter. Anyway, I’m here right now with coffee and painkillers, which I guess is something akin to Arseblog heritage.

    The Interlull is over and that’s it now until March. It’s non-stop Arsenal all the way, and all the focus will be on us and what we can produce on the pitch. For those interested in what our players got up to during this break, and what they delivered for their respective nations, Andrew A has a handy round-up over on Arseblog News. Now it’s about keeping everyone as fit as possible, the manager using the squad in the smartest and most effective way he can, and for some of the players who are capable of producing more doing exactly that.

    I was quite interested in Lewis’ quick look at Viktor Gyokeres and his key pass metrics from yesterday’s blog: He’s delivering a key pass every 28.4 minutes. Last season he had a key pass every 104 minutes across those two competitions [PL & CL].

    I think sample size might be a factor here, because when you look at his xG per 90, it’s 0.05 per 90 in both Premier League and Champions League this season, versus .99 and .76 per 90 last season, but obviously he played more minutes last time out. After 14 appearances this season, he’s rustled up a total of 614 minutes; this time last season his first 14 appearances brought him a cumulative 1200+ minutes. The absence of Kai Havertz was a factor, obviously, but it was probably that early season load that contributed to the injury he picked up against Burnley after a solid first half performance.

    Recent findings suggest that the job for Mikel Arteta is to find a way to share those minutes effectively, to have both his strikers scoring and assisting, and to harness some of what Gyokeres has been able to produce for Sweden. It’s often mooted that as a team we need to play to his strengths more, but perhaps these key pass metrics show that the design is more about eliminating some of the weaknesses in his game to make him more effective in the final third for us. Let’s see how it goes.

    Meanwhile, the KMI (Key Match Incident) panel have ruled on the Kai Havertz penalty incident against Hull. They ruled 5-0 that the on-field decision was wrong and that VAR, manned that day by Michael Oliver, should have intervened:.

    It has been revealed that although Havertz is clearly in an offside position, there is a clear and impactful holding action by Mendy before any potential offside offence by Havertz. Given the chronology of events, a penalty should have been awarded. The panel considered the VAR intervention was correct; however, the outcome after the on-field review was considered to be incorrect as a penalty should have been awarded.

    Industry observers note that I get every day is a learning day for ‘ProRef’, the people whose job it is to know the rules of football but week after week seem to demonstrate in newly introduced and inventive ways that they don’t. The question for us as fans is, what are we supposed to do with this? Are we supposed to feel better knowing that they’re owning up to mistakes? It feels a bit like getting run over when you have the green light at a pedestrian crossing, a nearby cop just lets the bloke go, but then later a judge claims he should have been stopped and arrested.

    Which is all well and good when you’re in a hospital bed in traction with a couple of broken legs and smashed pelvis (I say this only because I remember being in hospital with a bloke who fell under a bus and that’s what happened to him. He was fine though, his mates brought him in loads of joints which he used to share in the smoking room – this was 90s hospital). Which is to say, the damage has been done, the admission the bloke got it wrong in the first place doesn’t really make you feel any better.

    Sources indicate that from our perspective at least, Martin Odegaard’s winner ensured that decision didn’t turn out to be one which went on to live in infamy – like not drawing the lines for that Brentford goal that time, but it’s still essentially useless. Not least because you just know this weekend or next weekend some other mad thing will happen and they’ll say ‘Oooops! Sorry about that LOL here’s Michael Owen and Howard Webb!’, and some team will lose points because they can’t properly apply the rules of the game to things that happen on the pitch.

    Finally for today, we’re being linked with a January move for Bournemouth midfielder Alex Scott. He’s certainly a fine player, but it doesn’t make a lot of sense to me given we already have the best midfield depth in the Premier League, and beyond. Where does he fit with Declan Rice, Bruno Guimaraes, Martin Zubimendi, Mikel Merino, Myles Lewis-Skelly and Martin Odegaard? Perhaps if, for example, Zubi went there’s a case to be made for a replacement, but as it is he’s struggling for minutes anyway, and you don’t pay that kind of money for someone to come in and be peripheral.

    Sources indicate that like most of you, if there’s money to be spent in January, I’d much rather see it go on the forward line where I feel like there’s obvious room for improvement and to increase our depth. The left hand side is the obvious place, it’s hard not to worry about the right a little bit with Bukayo Saka’s injury, and the striker conversation is one which is never quite going to go away. So, on that basis, links to Scott don’t really add up for me. Unless Arteta fancies converting him to another left-back. Then it all clicks, but I think there’s one Bournemouth player we’d all rather see arrive.

    Sources indicate that right, I’m gonna leave it there for this morning. In terms of a podcast, I’m not quite feeling up to it today, but what we’ll do is make our Patreon preview podcast free and available to everyone tomorrow afternoon. I should be less sore then, and I continue to be blown away by your many emails and messages. Thank you so much, they mean the world.

    Mikel Arteta shuts down Arsenal team news loophole exposed by Christos Tzolis

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (857 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • By Naim Beneddra | 20 Nov 2026 18:48.
    • Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta has confirmed that fresh measures have been introduced to prevent players from accidentally revealing confidential team news through Fantasy Premier League (FPL).
    • The decision follows an incident involving Christos Tzolis, whose selections in the popular fantasy football game offered an unexpected insight into his availability ahead of Arsenal's Premier League victory over Liverpool earlier this month.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Naim Beneddra | 20 Nov 2026 18:48.

    Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta has confirmed that fresh measures have been introduced to prevent players from accidentally revealing confidential team news through Fantasy Premier League (FPL).

    The decision follows an incident involving Christos Tzolis, whose selections in the popular fantasy football game offered an unexpected insight into his availability ahead of Arsenal's Premier League victory over Liverpool earlier this month.

    According to The Athletic, Arsenal players have been banned from selecting themselves or their teammates in their FPL squads, reducing the risk of injuries and potential starting line-ups being disclosed before official announcements.

    Arteta confirmed the intervention during Friday's press conference ahead of Saturday's trip to Newcastle United, stressing that protecting information about his squad was essential to maintaining trust within the club.

    The development is particularly interesting given that Sports Mole was among the outlets to highlight Tzolis's revealing Fantasy Premier League decisions before Arsenal's visit to Anfield on November 1.

    Tzolis had been sidelined for approximately a month with a hamstring injury, missing six consecutive Arsenal matches before the trip to Liverpool.

    Although Arteta had confirmed that the Greek international had returned to training, his involvement at Anfield remained uncertain.

    However, the winger provided a significant indication of his fitness through his own Fantasy Premier League account.

    Tzolis transferred himself into his team and selected himself as captain, effectively doubling the points he would earn if he made a successful return.

    The decision attracted attention because fantasy managers generally avoid selecting injured players, particularly when using the captaincy on an individual who might not feature.

    Sports Mole had already identified the potential significance of those choices in its November 1 report on Tzolis's Fantasy Premier League injury clues.

    The same report noted that the former Norwich City winger had retained Riccardo Calafiori in his fantasy squad despite the defender also facing questions over his fitness.

    Both players subsequently started at Anfield, where Arsenal secured a 1-0 victory.

    Tzolis's activity attracted further attention in the following gameweek.

    Ahead of Arsenal's home meeting with Hull City on November 7, the 24-year-old reportedly activated his wildcard, allowing him to make unlimited transfers, and removed every Arsenal player from his fantasy team.

    Among those transferred out were Tzolis himself, Calafiori and Ezri Konsa.

    Those decisions did not establish who would or would not start against Hull, but they demonstrated how closely players' fantasy activity could be monitored for potential clues.

    Tzolis has also previously spoken openly about his enthusiasm for the game.

    After Arsenal's opening-day victory over Coventry City, he discussed the points he had accumulated through his own performance, revealing that he had selected himself as captain.

    What initially appeared to be a harmless aspect of the player's enjoyment of football has now prompted a response from his manager.

    Asked whether he had addressed the concern with his players, Arteta confirmed that discussions had taken place involving Tzolis and other members of the squad.

    "With Christos, with the squad and with my kids as well," the Arsenal manager remarked.

    It has been revealed that "They're constantly asking me about this as well, because they want to know. It's a topic.".

    Arteta acknowledged that the popularity of Fantasy Premier League had created a relatively new challenge for clubs seeking to protect information about their players.

    "These are the kind of things that are happening in our society right now," he explained.

    "It's something newly introduced. We haven't dealt with it before and we need to put new things in place.".

    The Spaniard then emphasised the importance of maintaining confidentiality within the dressing room and coaching staff.

    "The confidentiality is something critical because it's about trust and what you're trying to do, and that should be kept as a huge secret.".

    Arteta added that measures would be taken to prevent further incidents and subsequently confirmed that restrictions were already in place.

    The reported policy does not prevent Arsenal players from participating in Fantasy Premier League altogether.

    Instead, it specifically targets the selection of Arsenal footballers in their own fantasy teams, limiting the possibility that transfers or captaincy choices reveal information unavailable to opponents and supporters.

    Arsenal are not the first Premier League club to confront the problem.

    Chelsea faced similar concerns in October after fantasy accounts associated with players and staff appeared to offer clues about Joao Pedro's injury before his absence against Tottenham Hotspur became public.

    The Brazilian had reportedly been removed from several fantasy teams ahead of that fixture, prompting speculation about his availability.

    Chelsea subsequently warned staff about the risks of revealing confidential information through the game.

    For Arsenal, the issue is especially relevant as Arteta attempts to maintain his side's position at the top of the Premier League.

    The Gunners travel to Newcastle on Saturday with a five-point advantage over their nearest challengers, and the manager will be keen to avoid giving opponents unnecessary information about his selection decisions.

    Tzolis's fantasy activity may have provided an early indication of his return against Liverpool, but Arsenal's fresh restrictions are designed to ensure that future team news emerges through official channels rather than virtual football transfers.

    Observation of tunable superradiant frequency combs

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 52 min read (10331 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

    ⏱️ ~52 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Cavity quantum electrodynamics1 with quantum emitters coupled to resonators provides a powerful platform for engineering light–matter interactions2,3 and exploring many-body phenomena4,5.
    • Recent findings suggest that the invention of the laser stands among the most transformative technological advances of the twentieth century11.
    • Specifically, from a conceptual perspective, conventional lasers and superradiant light sources represent two complementary limits of light–matter interaction in a cavity-coupled system.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Cavity quantum electrodynamics1 with quantum emitters coupled to resonators provides a powerful platform for engineering light–matter interactions2,3 and exploring many-body phenomena4,5. In particular, superradiance6—arising from collective quantum interference among emitters—has been explored as a route to ultrastable continuous radiation7. However, engineering superradiance in the time domain to realize periodic pulsed sources or frequency combs remains largely unexplored. Here we investigate the non-equilibrium many-body dynamics of a driven spin ensemble coupled with an on-chip superconducting resonator and uncover a dynamical phase transition from continuous-wave to periodic pulsed superradiant emission. To quantitatively capture the observed dynamical phases, we introduce a driven-dissipative cavity-quantum electrodynamics model that elucidates how the periodic pulsed superradiant phase emerges from collective, periodically repeating spin dynamics stabilized by the interplay of coherence growth, disorder and dissipation. We also find that rare-earth ion spin systems with both optical and microwave transitions enable phase-synchronized, dual-rail superradiant frequency combs in both the microwave and the optical domains. Our results not only open upcoming opportunities for atom-based frequency-comb sources and programmable superradiant generation, but establish a fundamental connection between periodic pulsed superradiance and the emergence of a continuous time crystal8,9,10 as a new non-equilibrium phase in driven open systems.

    Recent findings suggest that the invention of the laser stands among the most transformative technological advances of the twentieth century11. Laser operation relies on stimulated emission, whereby coherent radiation emerges once the gain exceeds loss in a resonant cavity12. By contrast, superradiance, first proposed by Dicke in 195413, can also lead to continuous coherent radiation arising from a collective many-body dissipation process in which emission results from quantum interference among an ensemble of emitters6. Remarkably, compared with conventional lasers, superradiant emission can have exceptional frequency stability due to the long coherence of atomic transitions, along with output power that scales nonlinearly with ensemble size7. Superradiance has been observed across a wide range of platforms in both free space and cavity-coupled systems, including cold atoms14,15,16, atomic gases17,18, artificial atoms19,20,21 and solid-state defects22,23,24.

    Specifically, from a conceptual perspective, conventional lasers and superradiant light sources represent two complementary limits of light–matter interaction in a cavity-coupled system. Conventional lasers rely on stimulated emission, where the coherence is governed primarily by the cavity field. Superradiant systems, however, operate in the opposite regime, where coherence resides predominantly in the atomic ensemble, and radiation emerges from collectively synchronized dissipation driven by atom–atom correlations mediated by a lossy (bad) cavity (Fig. 1a–c). In this regime, the dynamics are naturally described within the framework of cavity quantum electrodynamics (QED), where light–matter interactions are treated at the fundamental quantum-mechanical level and different photon emission mechanisms can be individually identified25. This perspective has motivated extensive studies on superradiant dynamics in cavity QED systems1,2,26,27, including superradiant bursts28,29, triggered superradiance30 and ultra-narrow-linewidth superradiant lasers7,31,32.

    a, An ensemble of two-level atoms, \(\{| \uparrow \rangle ,| \downarrow \rangle \}\), coupled with a common cavity field. The cavity output serves simultaneously as a probe of the intracavity dynamics and as an emitted light field generated by the atomic ensemble. b, The frequency–domain picture for a superradiant, bad-cavity regime, where the inhomogeneously broadened atomic linewidth, Γ, is narrower than the cavity linewidth, κ. c, A comparison table between conventional and superradiant light sources. d, Three types of superradiant dynamics: superradiant burst emission under a transient pump (di), steady superradiant emission under a continuous-wave (CW) pump (dii), and periodic pulsed superradiant emission under a continuous-wave pump (diii). In diii, as the cavity coupling strength increases, periodic pulsed emission dynamics emerge due to the spontaneous breaking of continuous time-translation symmetry under a continuous-wave drive. We find that the periodicity, T, of the pulsed emission is set by the ensemble cooperativity, whereas the onset time, t0, of the resulting pulse train relative to the start of the continuous-wave drive is spontaneously random. e, A phase diagram of a cavity QED model showing three distinct phases of no superradiance (SR) (I), continuous-wave superradiance (CW SR) (II) and periodic superradiance (III). These phases are distinguished by the interplay of cavity-mediated collective coupling and dissipation, and disorder due to the frequency inhomogeneity of the emitters. The coutinuous-wave superradiance phase emerges when the ensemble cooperativity exceeds unity (C = 1, black solid line), whereas the periodic superradiance phase is expected to emerge when the normalized cavity–ensemble coupling strength exceeds unity (gnorm = 1, black dashed line). Surprisingly, the phase transition into the periodic superradiance phase occurs at a weaker coupling strength in our experiment due to the presence of disorder, consistent with our theoretical prediction (red solid line). The yellow vertical bar indicates the experimentally probed regime of collective coupling strengths (refer to the main text and Supplementary Information for details).

    Historically, advances in laser physics have demonstrated that introducing nonlinear elements can drive systems into unstable dynamical regimes33, enabling the development of mode-locked lasers that generate periodic, ultrafast optical pulses34. This periodic emission in the time domain, corresponding to a frequency comb in the spectral domain, dramatically expands the impact of lasers across science and industry35,36. This naturally raises curiosity into whether superradiant systems can support frequency-comb-like emission that produces time-periodic, phase-coherent pulse trains, and if so, what mechanism underlies this behaviour, and whether the resulting time-domain pulsing can be engineered.

    Industry observers note that although recent theoretical37 and experimental38,39 efforts have begun to explore periodic pulsed superradiant dynamics in driven-dissipative systems, a clear understanding of their physical origin and underlying mechanisms, as well as comprehensive experimental demonstrations, remains elusive. Here we develop a unified theoretical and experimental framework that elucidates how superradiant frequency combs emerge in a driven cavity QED system of quantum emitters through the interplay of atomic coherence, dissipation and disorder, where the nonlinearity is provided by superradiant emission. Building on this framework, we experimentally investigate non-equilibrium superradiant dynamics in a disordered spin ensemble coupled to a superconducting microwave cavity, and show that robust, phase-coherent superradiant pulse trains can be both probed and engineered, with their pulse repetition rate set by the ensemble cooperativity. Unexpectedly, we also observe simultaneous and correlated periodic microwave and optical superradiant emissions that are both time-synchronized and phase-coherent. We refer to this phenomenon as dual-rail superradiant frequency combs, which opens new opportunities for ensemble-based quantum technologies. Furthermore, our results reveal a fundamental connection to a continuous time crystal, that is, a dynamical phase of matter in driven, non-equilibrium cavity QED systems characterized by spontaneously broken continuous time-translation symmetry and the emergence of robust temporal order.

    Recent findings suggest that to develop an intuitive understanding of the physical origin and mechanisms underlying superradiant frequency-comb formation, we consider an ensemble of frequency-inhomogeneous two-level quantum emitters (\(| \downarrow \rangle ,| \uparrow \rangle \)) coupled to a common lossy cavity mode and driven by an external pump. The microscopic dynamics of such cavity–ensemble interactions are imprinted on the cavity output, which serves as the primary experimentally accessible observable of the system’s cavity QED behaviour. Specifically, the photon emission rate, Γph, is governed by three distinct emission processes: Purcell-enhanced spontaneous emission, stimulated emission and superradiant emission25:.

    Here g is the single atom-cavity coupling strength; κ is the cavity decay rate; N is the number of quantum emitters; \({\widehat{S}}_{z}=\frac{1}{2}{\sum }_{j}{\widehat{\sigma }}_{z,j}\) is the collective spin operator along the z direction, representing the total population imbalance of the ensemble with \({\widehat{\sigma }}_{z,j}={| \downarrow \rangle }_{j}\langle \downarrow | -{| \uparrow \rangle }_{j}\langle \uparrow | \) for the jth spin; \({\widehat{S}}_{\downarrow \uparrow }={\sum }_{j}{\widehat{\sigma }}_{\downarrow \uparrow ,j}\) and \({\widehat{S}}_{\uparrow \downarrow }={\widehat{S}}_{\downarrow \uparrow }^{\dagger }\) represent the collective ensemble coherence obtained from the sum of individual atomic coherences, with \({\widehat{\sigma }}_{\downarrow \uparrow ,j}={| \downarrow \rangle }_{j}\langle \uparrow | \); and \(\widehat{b}\) and \({\widehat{b}}^{\dagger }\) are the cavity annihilation and creation operators, respectively (Methods).

    Recent findings suggest that in contrast to conventional laser systems, where emission is dominated by stimulated emission (second term in equation (1)), superradiant systems are governed by collective spin correlations (third term), with the photon emission rate scaling as \(\langle {\widehat{S}}_{\uparrow \downarrow }{\widehat{S}}_{\downarrow \uparrow }\rangle \propto {N}^{2}\). This collective behaviour acts as an effective nonlinearity, providing the foundation for dynamical phase transitions in superradiance.

    Although three different mechanisms contribute to the photon emission rate, the presence of superradiant dynamics can first be identified by monitoring the emission following a transient excitation pump pulse (Fig. 1di). In this case, superradiant ensembles have a delayed burst of emission arising from stochastic quantum fluctuations that initiate synchronized dissipation of individual emitters, providing a clear signature of superradiance14,28.

    It has been revealed that transitioning from a transient pump to a continuous-wave pump, the superradiant ensemble can support continuous emission by reaching a steady-state condition under the continuous-wave pump (Fig. 1dii). Analogous to a conventional laser, this condition is achieved when the cavity-mediated gain, \(\frac{4N{g}^{2}}{\kappa }\), is greater than the atomic dephasing rate, Γ (here, Γ is the linewidth of the emitter ensemble). Equivalently, defining the ensemble cooperativity as \(C=\frac{4N{g}^{2}}{\kappa \varGamma }\), continuous-wave superradiant emission occurs when C ≥ 1 (Fig. 1e, solid black line).

    In a recent development, crucially, when the coherent cavity–ensemble coupling strength, \(\sqrt{N}g\), exceeds the cavity-induced decoherence rate, κ/2, the steady-state dynamics can break down, turning continuous-wave into periodic pulsed emission (Fig. 1diii and Fig. 1e, dashed black line). In this regime, quantum interference between the strongly dressed cavity–ensemble states drives oscillatory behaviour in the photon emission. Surprisingly, however, we find that the presence of moderate disorder (defined as an extra inhomogeneous contribution to spectral line broadening beyond the homogeneous linewidth) substantially lowers the critical coupling threshold, thereby facilitating the phase transition into the pulsed phase (Fig. 1e, solid red line). Refer to the Supplementary Information for details on the theoretical phase boundary, which is estimated on the basis of a Hopf bifurcation model.

    Using our driven-dissipative cavity QED model, we elucidate how such periodic pulsed emission directly originates from an emergent, time-periodic trajectory of the spin ensemble, in which collective coherence builds up, collapses through synchronized dissipation, and is then rebuilt under continuous pumping (inset of Fig. 1diii). We find from both our experiment and the theoretical model that this persistent pulsed emission repeats robustly without decay, with a periodicity, T ∝ 1/C, set by the ensemble cooperativity, C. This periodic superradiance phase, arising intrinsically and spontaneously from time-independent cavity QED dynamics, stands in stark contrast to conventional mode-locked lasers, where the periodicity is externally imposed by the cavity round-trip time. Such spontaneously broken time-translation symmetry, leading to the emergence of temporal order, defines a continuous time crystal—a class of non-equilibrium phases of matter that has been explored in a variety of driven-dissipative systems8,9,10,40.

    We use rare-earth-ion-doped crystals to experimentally explore superradiant dynamics; such crystals offer highly coherent transitions in both the microwave and optical domains at cryogenic temperatures41,42, and are readily compatible with on-chip cavity QED architectures43,44,45,46. In particular, we use an ensemble of ytterbium-171 ions doped in a yttrium orthovanadate crystal47, whose excited-state spin manifold forms a two-level system, \(\{|\uparrow \rangle ,|\downarrow \rangle \}\), with a microwave transition frequency of ω = 2π × 3.4 GHz and an inhomogeneously broadened linewidth of Γ = 2π × 160 kHz (Fig. 2a). A superconducting microwave resonator with a cavity linewidth of κ = 2π × 3.6 MHz is fabricated on the crystal to couple to the excited-state microwave spin transition. We measured a maximum collective coupling strength of \(\sqrt{N}g\approx 2{\rm{\pi }}\times 1.1\) MHz, corresponding to a normalized coupling strength of \({g}_{{\rm{norm}}}=2\sqrt{N}g/\kappa \approx 0.6\), which lies below the critical threshold necessary for inducing the periodic superradiant phase in the absence of disorder (Extended Data Fig. 1).

A continuous-wave optical pump controls the net population in the two-level microwave spin manifold, \(\{|\downarrow \rangle ,|\uparrow \rangle \}\), by driving optical transitions between \(|g\rangle \) and \(|\uparrow \rangle \). Thus, the collective coupling strength, which scales with N, can be readily tuned by varying the pump power. A superconducting microwave resonator (red) couples the \(|\downarrow \rangle \leftrightarrow |\uparrow \rangle \) transition at around 3.4 GHz. A weak optical Fabry–Pérot mode (yellow) at about 304 THz couples the optical transitions (refer to Fig. 4 for transferred optical superradiance). b, Bloch-sphere representations of superradiant dynamics in three distinct regimes (I, no superradiance (SR); II, continuous-wave superradiance (CW SR); III, periodic superradiance) probed with increasing collective coupling strength. In regime I, the collective coupling is too weak to generate ensemble coherence, resulting in no superradiance. In regime II, a stable balance among cavity-induced coherence growth (red arrows), disorder-induced precession (blue arrows) and dephasing (black arrows) stabilizes continuous superradiant emission for all individual spins. Five spins are depicted representatively. In regime III, the continuous-wave superradiance phase becomes unstable due to increased coupling strength, driving the spin system into a phase characterized by persistent, periodic pulsed emission dynamics. The periodic behaviour originates from a stable limit cycle, characterized by recurring cycles of coherence growth, precession and dephasing. c, Time-domain superradiance emission profiles for the three regimes, as the continuous-wave pump power increases from 0  to 36 μW (refer to the Methods for measurement details). d, Corresponding Fourier spectra for the three regimes. Insets in regimes II and III show linewidths of approximately 30 and 50 Hz, respectively, which are about three orders of magnitude narrower than the spin inhomogeneous linewidth (about 160 kHz). e, Microwave superradiant emission power as a function of continuous-wave pump strength. The corresponding normalized collective coupling strength, gnorm, is shown on the top x axis (Fig. 1e, yellow line, and Extended Data Fig. 1). Black (blue) points denote the total (sideband) spectral power, Atot (Asb). The phase transitions into the continuous-wave and periodic phases are marked by sharp increases in Atot and Asb, respectively. The inset demonstrates the time-crystalline fraction, Asb/Atot, providing a clear distinction between the continuous-wave and periodic superradiance phases as a function of pump power.

    Importantly, although the total available number of ytterbium ions in the cavity is on the order of Ntot ≈ 4 × 1010, we can control the effective emitter number, N ≤ Ntot, which participates in superradiant dynamics by varying the optical pump power that transfers population to the \(|\uparrow \rangle \) state in the excited-state manifold (Fig. 2a). We experimentally verify that superradiance dominates the dynamics of our dense cavity-coupled spin ensemble by observing that the delay time (τd) of a superradiant burst under a transient pump scales inversely with the effective ensemble size, N, that is, τd ∝ 1/N (Extended Data Fig. 2). Notably, by simply varying the continuous-wave pump power, we can continuously tune the ensemble cooperativity, thereby enabling systematic exploration of superradiant dynamics and phase transitions across three distinct regimes: no superradiance (regime I), continuous-wave superradiance (regime II) and periodic superradiance (regime III) (Fig. 2b; Fig. 1e, yellow line).

    According to recent reports, we first probe non-equilibrium dynamics under a weak continuous-wave pump at low collective cavity coupling strength. In this regime, the \(|\uparrow \rangle \)-state population is insufficient to establish collective behaviour, and no superradiant emission occurs (Fig. 2c,d, regime I).

    It has been revealed that however, as the pump power increases and crosses the critical threshold at which the ensemble cooperativity exceeds unity, a steady-state coherence emerges in this non-equilibrium setting, giving rise to continuous-wave superradiance (regime II). Intuitively, in the Bloch-sphere picture, this can be understood as a balance of competing contributions acting on each spin, where disorder, dephasing and coherence growth terms compensate one another, resulting in a collectively enhanced steady-state coherence (Fig. 2b, regime II). In the Fourier spectrum, we find that the emission linewidth is around 30 Hz—a value that is orders of magnitude narrower than the inhomogeneous ensemble linewidth (Fig. 2d, regime II; Extended Data Fig. 3).

    Sources indicate that upon further increasing the pump power, and thus the collective coupling strength, we observe that the continuous-wave superradiant emission becomes unstable, leading to a breakdown of the balance, which in turn gives rise to time-periodic pulsed emission dynamics (regime III). Essentially, a stronger pump provides a larger nonlinear perturbation in the collective ensemble coherence, which triggers synchronized dissipation across the entire spin ensemble. The decayed emitters are then repumped into the excited state, forming a closed, repeating cycle that generates a persistent superradiant pulse train (Fig. 2c, regime III). This behaviour can also be understood as a Hopf bifurcation that signals the breakdown of steady-state dynamics and leads to the emergence of a stable limit cycle8. In the spectral domain we observe a frequency-comb structure with a narrow comb linewidth of about 50 Hz, indicating stable phase coherence of the pulses (Fig. 2d, regime III).

    We analyse the emission spectrum in detail to systematically determine the phase boundaries across the three distinct superradiant phases (Fig. 2e). Specifically, we define the total emitted spectral power as \({A}_{{\rm{tot}}}={\int }_{-\infty }^{+\infty }S(\omega )d\omega \), and the total sideband power as \({A}_{{\rm{sb}}}={\int }_{-\infty }^{{\omega }_{p}-\Delta \omega /2}S(\omega )d\omega +{\int }_{{\omega }_{p}+\Delta \omega /2}^{+\infty }S(\omega )d\omega \), where S(ω) is the power spectral density of the time-domain emission signal, ωp is the frequency corresponding to the peak spectral density and Δω is a narrow integration window that isolates the central spectral peak. These quantities serve as effective experimental order parameters that distinguish the three phases in our experiment. Concretely, the onset of continuous-wave superradiance (regimes I to II) is marked by a sharp increase in Atot, whereas the transition from the continuous-wave to the pulsed superradiant phase (regimes II to III) is signalled by a sharp increase in Asb. To more clearly characterize the second phase transition, we introduce the normalized sideband fraction, which is defined as the ratio Asb/Atot. This quantity, which has also been used to characterize the crystalline fraction in time-crystal phenomena8,48, provides a clear signature of the transition into the periodic superradiant phase (Fig. 2e, inset).

    In a recent development, crucially, this robust temporal ordering in the superradiant dynamics emerges spontaneously under strictly time-independent continuous-wave pumping, without any externally imposed modulation or timing reference. By repeating the experiment under identical conditions, we find that the onset time of the superradiant pulse train is spontaneously random from experiment to experiment (Extended Data Fig. 4), providing direct evidence of the spontaneous breaking of continuous time-translation symmetry8. Our experimental measurements and numerical simulations consistently indicate that the system satisfies the defining criteria of a time-crystalline phase (Extended Data Table 1).

    Recent findings suggest that A natural follow-up investigation would be to determine what sets the periodicity of the persistent, periodic superradiant phase. According to our theoretical framework, the periodicity of the superradiant bursts is determined by the ensemble cooperativity, which depends on the number of emitters participating in the superradiant dynamics. To probe this experimentally, we selectively excite different spectral subsets of ytterbium ions by intentionally detuning the pump carrier frequency across an optical inhomogeneous linewidth of about 2π × 92 MHz. This allows us to systematically vary the number of emitters excited to the \(|\uparrow \rangle \) state within the microwave superradiant manifold while keeping the pump Rabi frequency unchanged (Fig. 3a).

    In a recent development, a, Optical inhomogeneous broadening profile with a linewidth of about 2π × 92 MHz for Ntot ≈ 4 × 1010 ions in our system. By tuning the continuous-wave pump detuning, Δpump, relative to the ensemble centre frequency, different spectral subsets of spins are selectively pumped into the excited-state manifold, enabling continuous control of the effective ensemble size that participates in superradiance. b, Measured phase diagram showing superradiant emission (red, regimes II and III) and no superradiance (blue, regime I) phases under varying pump detuning and power. The dashed line indicates the calculated phase boundary corresponding to an ensemble cooperativity of 1. c, Time-domain microwave superradiant bursts recorded at various pump detunings under 36 μW pump power. The superradiant burst periodicity, T, varies systematically with pump detuning. d, Numerical simulations of the periodic superradiant phase based on the same experimental conditions used in c, showing good agreement between theory and experiment. e, Detuning-resolved experimental time traces from c at pump detunings of Δpump/2π = 2.4, 12, 18.4, 26.4, 31.2 and 36 MHz, illustrating how periodicity and emission intensity vary with detuning. Darker (fainter) colours correspond to smaller (larger) detuning values. f, Rescaled time traces from e, demonstrating universal data collapse (refer to the main text for details).

    Industry observers note that as shown in Fig. 3b, the threshold for the onset of superradiant emission increases as the optical pump is detuned away from the centre of the inhomogeneous linewidth, indicating that pump detuning serves as an effective control knob for tuning the collective cavity–ensemble coupling strength. In regime III we observe that the superradiant burst periodicity, T, also depends sensitively on the pump detuning (Fig. 3c): T increases as the detuning moves away from zero. Numerical simulations show strong quantitative agreement with our experimental observations, further corroborating the effective tuning of the collective coupling strength via pump detuning in our system (Fig. 3d and Extended Data Fig. 5).

    As our theoretical framework reveals that T scales inversely with the ensemble size N, while the intensity scales quadratically with N, we rescale both the time and intensity axes of all measured superradiant burst profiles, acquired at different detuning values, by their corresponding effective ensemble size. Remarkably, we find that all data collapse onto a single universal curve (Fig. 3e,f). This universal collapse demonstrates that the periodic superradiant phase is governed by collective scaling laws set by the effective size of the driven spin ensemble, independent of the microscopic details of individual emitters.

    Collectively, our experimental findings, in agreement with our theoretical model, indicate that the periodic superradiant phase is a robust collective phenomenon representing a non-equilibrium phase of matter in driven open quantum systems. To further substantiate this, we perform extensive numerical simulations addressing the following three key aspects (Extended Data Fig. 6). First, we confirm that, in our experimental regime, the nonlinear superradiant term associated with collective ensemble correlations dominates the conventional stimulated emission term by more than an order of magnitude. Second, we verify that the observed pulsed phase originates from a large atomic ensemble, as it cannot be explained by a single emitter with an artificially enhanced coupling strength. Third, we demonstrate that disorder plays an essential role, as the periodic superradiant phase does not emerge in the absence of disorder for the experimentally measured coupling strength, gnorm ≈ 0.6. This finding implies that inhomogeneous broadening is not merely a source of decoherence, but can instead be harnessed to engineer collective quantum interference, thereby reshaping photon-emission dynamics in the cavity QED system.

    Industry observers note that although our experimental results so far have focused on superradiance in the microwave domain, our ytterbium-ion-based system intrinsically comprises a three-level structure that involves both microwave and optical transitions. Direct optical superradiance is not observed due to the low optical cooperativity49 (of about 0.14). However, we find that the periodic superradiant dynamics in the microwave transition is transferred to the optical transition via a coherent Raman scattering process50 (\(|g\rangle \langle \uparrow |\cdot | \uparrow \rangle \langle \downarrow |\Rightarrow |g\rangle \langle \downarrow |\)). Consequently, the transferred optical field coherently inherits the temporal dynamics of the microwave field, giving rise to correlated, dual-rail frequency-comb generation in both the microwave and optical domains (Extended Data Figs. 7 and 8). As shown in Fig. 4a, the optical and microwave signals have temporally synchronized burst sequences, demonstrating that both emissions originate from the same underlying collective dynamics. To quantify the coherence between the two emission channels, we analyse their relative phase difference and observe a zero-phase offset, indicating in-phase locking across the microwave and optical domains (Fig. 4b). We further characterize the spectra of the dual-rail frequency combs and confirm that the narrow comb structures are well matched and have the same repetition rate (Fig. 4c).

    a, Simultaneously recorded microwave and optical superradiant burst emissions under 200-μW pump power over a 500-μs window, showing time-synchronized pulsed superradiance emission. The overlays represent the signal amplitudes after demodulation (Fig. 2a). Mixers with a local oscillator (LO) are used for measurement (Methods; refer to Extended Data Fig. 7 for measurements taken over a 100-ms window, and Extended Data Fig. 8 for phase-stability analysis). b, Relative phase difference between microwave (ϕMW) and optical (ϕOP) superradiant bursts. The phases of individual pulses are analysed using a magnified 20 μs window on each burst within a 2 ms continuous measurement frame, revealing strong in-phase correlation, that is, ϕMW − ϕOP ≈ 0 with a s.d. of about 0.06π, across the two emission channels. c, Emission spectrum of the transferred optical superradiance (yellow), overlaid with that of the microwave superradiance (blue, identical to that shown in Fig. 2d), revealing a spectrally overlapping frequency-comb structure.

    Industry observers note that our work positions disordered solid-state cavity QED systems as a versatile platform at the intersection of cavity QED, non-equilibrium physics and quantum metrology. A central result is a unified understanding of dynamical phase transitions in a driven cavity QED system, where the periodic pulsed superradiant phase can be identified as a continuous time-crystal phase. We also demonstrate the unexpected observation and tunable engineering of robust dual-rail superradiant frequency combs in both the microwave and optical domains. We believe these results pave the way for stable atom-based frequency comb sources, superradiance-based waveform synthesis and coherent microwave-optical quantum interconnects.

    Sources indicate that our platform opens several promising avenues for future exploration. The repetition rate is at the moment limited by the optical pumping rate required to rebuild population inversion. Incorporating a high-cooperativity optical cavity would Purcell-enhance the repumping process, which would increase the transferred optical emission strength and enable higher repetition rates and faster control over ensemble participation, while also allowing direct generation of a tunable optical superradiant frequency comb. In parallel, recent advances in superconducting microwave technology offer new opportunities to dynamically engineer the cavity-mediated interactions that govern the collective dynamics. Combined control over ensemble coupling, dissipation and detuning will unlock a powerful route to programmable quantum light sources, enabling on-demand synthesis of tailored emission waveforms and new paradigms in coherent quantum control.

    According to recent reports, 171Yb3+:YVO4 crystals are grown by Gamdan Optics and further diced into 6 mm × 6 mm × 0.5 mm chips. The ytterbium-171 concentration is measured to be 340 ppm via secondary ion mass spectrometry. A 150-nm niobium film is sputtered onto the chip surface at 3.5 mTorr. The device patterns are written by an electron beam lithography system (Raith EBPG 5200) with an ma-N 2403 photoresist. A 25-nm aluminium layer was evaporated as a hard mask, followed by further lift-off using remover PG. The niobium was dry-etched in a plasma-reactive ion etcher, and the aluminium mask was removed using a wet-etching process with aluminium etchant and 3.5% hydrofluoric acid. Finally, a 100-nm gold layer is evaporated on the back of the chip to form a reflective coating.

    A master laser (Toptica DL Pro) is locked to a stable cavity reference (Stable laser systems) via the Pound–Drever–Hall method, resulting in an approximately 22 kHz locking linewidth. The experimental laser (Moglabs CEL) is offset-locked to the master laser using a Vescent D2-135 servo and TPI 1005-A frequency source for further tuning the locking frequency. This frequency source is frequency-locked to a 10 MHz rubidium frequency standard (SRS FS725) with a specified phase noise below −130 dBc Hz–1 at a 10 Hz offset. The chip is mounted on the mixing-chamber plate of a dilution refrigerator (Bluefors LD250). A total of 70-dB attenuation is distributed along the microwave input lines. The microwave output line is connected to cryogenic circulators (LNF-CIC2.8-4.3A) at the mixing chamber plate and linked to a high-electron-mobility transistor amplifier (LNF-LNC2-6B) at 4 K plate via superconducting coax cables. The microwave signal outside the fridge is measured on a Field Fox N9915A spectrum analyser and an oscilloscope (Tektronix TDS7104). For pulsed measurements, a digitizer (Alazar ATS9130) is used to acquire data after mixing down to 5 MHz with an IQ mixer (Marki Microwave IQ0307 LXP). When analysing the total sideband power Asb, we use Δω = 2π × 10 kHz to fully isolate the central spectral peak from adjacent sidebands. The memory depth of our acquisition instrument for IQ detection limits the longest continuously recorded single-shot trace to 100 ms (Extended Data Fig. 7). However, we observe no discernible decay in the periodic superradiance over several hours of data acquisition each day.

    Industry observers note that the optical pump is delivered into the device through a pair of aspheric lenses and collected along the same path via the gold layer reflection. The beam is focused on the gold layer with a 4-μm beam waist, resulting in a 20-μm beam waist on the front surface of the chip for the experiment. The collected optical photons are combined with another optical path outside the fridge from the same experiment laser for heterodyne measurements at a 200-MHz offset frequency, which is also frequency-locked to the rubidium frequency standard. The optical heterodyne signal is detected by a high-speed photodiode (ALPHALAS UPD-35-IR-2) and further analysed using Field Fox N9115A spectrum analyser, or down-converted to 5 MHz with an IQ mixer (Marki Microwave IQ0307 LXP) and measured on Tektronix TDS7104 oscilloscope. For pulsed excitations, an acousto-optic modulator (Aerodiode model 6) shapes the optical pump beam with a trigger from Zurich HDAWG. All electronics used in experiments are externally referenced to the 10-MHz rubidium frequency standard. All of the relevant experimental parameters can be found in Extended Data Table 2.

    For the phase coherence analysed in Extended Data Fig. 8, we record the IQ traces of the microwave and optical field, I(t) and Q(t), using the four channels of an oscilloscope (Tektronix TDS7104). We reconstruct the complex heterodyne field as Z(t) = I(t) + iQ(t) = A(t)eiϕ(t), where A(t) and ϕ(t) are the amplitude and phase at time t, respectively. By centring each pulse in the time-domain pulse-train traces, we estimate the standard deviation of the pulse-to-pulse phase (normalized amplitude) variations to be 0.03π (0.009) and 0.11π (0.05) for the microwave and optical fields, respectively (Extended Data Fig. 8b,d). We note that the transferred optical superradiant pulse train follows the microwave-domain pulse train as a result of the coherent Raman scattering process. The larger standard deviation of the optical superradiant pulse train is probably dominated by the higher detection noise floor and the phase instability of the optical heterodyne set-up.

    In the bad cavity regime, where the cavity decay rate, κ, is much greater than the collective coupling strength, \(\sqrt{N}g\), we can adiabatically eliminate the cavity field, which yields a reduced set of equations of motion involving only the spin degrees of freedom:.

In the presence of ensemble coherence, spin inversion (\(\langle {\widehat{\sigma }}_{z,k}\rangle < 0\)), acting in tandem, leads to the growth of individual spin coherence. At the collective level, the ensemble polarization dynamics, \(\langle {\mathop{\widehat{{S}}}\limits^{.}}_{z}\rangle \), depends on \(\langle {\widehat{S}}_{\uparrow \downarrow }\rangle \langle {\widehat{S}}_{\downarrow \uparrow }\rangle \), which is responsible for superradiant decay when this term is dominant. The full theoretical formalism and simulations—including both the optical and microwave cavities and their corresponding mean-field equations—can be found in Supplementary Section 1.

    Although the mean-field equations provide a leading-order, intuitive understanding of superradiant cavity QED dynamics with a disordered spin ensemble, the numerically simulated periodicity of pulsed superradiance is inconsistent with the experimental observations (Supplementary Information).

    In a recent development, our theoretical framework predicts how the burst periodicity (T), peak power (Ppeak) and average emission power (\({\overline{P}}_{{\rm{MW}}}\)) scale with the number of participating emitters, N (Extended Data Fig. 5a). First, the burst periodicity is governed by the ensemble cooperativity, leading to the scaling of T ∝ 1/N (Extended Data Fig. 5b). Second, each burst originates from the collective emission of an inverted ensemble of N atoms, resulting in the emission of N photons. As the superradiant burst duration, τw, scales inversely with the ensemble size, that is, τw ∝ 1/N, the peak power—proportional to the burst energy divided by its duration—scales quadratically with N, that is, Ppeak ∝ N2 (Extended Data Fig. 5c). Third, the average emission power follows from the burst energy multiplied by the repetition rate, leading to the same quadratic scaling with N, that is, \({\overline{P}}_{{\rm{MW}}}\propto {N}^{2}\) (Extended Data Fig. 5d).

    It has been revealed that as shown in Extended Data Fig. 5, all of these scaling predictions are in excellent agreement with the experimental data. This agreement enables a universal rescaling of the experimentally observed superradiant pulse trains in terms of the effective ensemble size N, or equivalently, the experimentally tunable cooperativity.

    The emission linewidth of a superradiant atomic ensemble has been studied extensively in the literature, both in the thermal ground-state and finite-temperature regimes54,55. By linearizing the quantum Langevin equations in the frequency domain, one can compute the phase fluctuation correlation function of the emitted field and hence derive the emission linewidth as.

    where nc is the intracavity photon number; κc and κa are the linewidths of the cavity mode and atomic ensemble, respectively; nth is the thermal occupancy of the cavity mode; and nsp is the spontaneous emission factor. The linewidth is therefore determined by noise contributions from both the thermal bath of the cavity mode and the imperfect inversion of the atomic ensemble. In the ideal limit of a quantum ground state with perfect population inversion, one recovers the result of ref. 7 by setting nth = nsp = 0. Noting that the emission power P is proportional to the intracavity photon number, that is, P ∝ nc, the linewidth correspondingly narrows as ΔfST ∝ 1/P.

    By fitting equation (13) to the data shown in Extended Data Fig. 3, we extract a total noise contribution of nth + nsp = 5.8 quanta. From numerical simulations, the spontaneous emission factor is estimated to be nsp = 2.6 quanta, leaving nth = 3.2 quanta for the thermal occupancy of the microwave resonator, corresponding to an effective resonator temperature of around 0.6 K.

    It has been revealed that we also observe a correlation between the microwave and optical transition frequencies, consistent with previous observations56. The laser linewidth is carefully calibrated using the Pound–Drever–Hall error signal, yielding a locking linewidth of 22 kHz. This corresponds to a 27 Hz limit on the microwave emission frequency, as shown in Extended Data Fig. 3b.

    On the optical side, the transferred superradiant emission inherits the linewidth of the optical pump laser due to energy conservation. The data shown in Fig. 4c of the main text correspond to heterodyne detection between the optical emission and the pump laser, which in principle should yield the same linewidth as the microwave comb (about 50 Hz). However, the measured optical comb linewidth is about 1 kHz, probably due to frequency jitter arising from the time delay between the optical path through the dilution refrigerator and the local oscillator path.

    We evaluate whether the observed periodic pulsed superradiance can be classified as a continuous time-crystal phase by applying a set of five criteria commonly associated with time-crystalline order8,9,10,40,48.

    First, the underlying Hamiltonian should be time-independent, ensuring that any emergent periodic behaviour is not trivially imposed by external driving. Second, the observed dynamics should arise from genuine many-body dynamics, rather than from single-particle effects or externally enforced synchronization. Third, the system should have persistent and well-defined periodic temporal behaviour in its steady state. Fourth, this periodicity should correspond to the spontaneous breaking of continuous time-translation symmetry, meaning that the system evolves with a characteristic frequency that is not explicitly set by the Hamiltonian. Fifth, the observed behaviour should be robust against perturbations such as noise, dissipation and experimental imperfections, indicating the presence of a stable dynamical phase rather than fine-tuned transient dynamics.

    In a recent development, we systematically evaluate these criteria across different experimental platforms and summarize the results in Extended Data Table 1. This comparison provides a unified framework for assessing whether periodic superradiant dynamics can be understood within the broader context of continuous time crystals.

    To further corroborate that our system spontaneously breaks continuous time-translational symmetry, we apply a transient optical pump for 1 ms and monitor the emergence of the periodic pulsed-emission phase. The temporal phase, θk, of the continuous time crystal is defined from the onset time of the periodic burst oscillations as θk = 2π × τk/T (mod 2π), where k indexes individual experimental realizations and τk is the burst onset time in the kth run. As shown in Extended Data Fig. 4, the system first undergoes superradiant burst dynamics and then relaxes into a long-lived periodic pulsed phase that persists without decay over the observation window. Crucially, the onset time, and hence the phase θk, varies randomly over 2π across repeated experiments, indicating that the phase is not determined by the transient pump. This self-evolved randomness provides evidence that temporal order emerges spontaneously, consistent with the spontaneous breaking of continuous time-translational symmetry.

    Furthermore, as shown in Extended Data Fig. 7, the observed periodic superradiance represents a robust dynamical phase in which both microwave superradiance and the transferred optical superradiance exhibit essentially non-decaying oscillations under continuous pumping.
